options.D: The effectiveness of black-box test techniques depends heavily on the individual tester's skill, more so than white-box or experience-based techniques

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states that the effectiveness of EXPERIENCE-BASED techniques depends heavily on the tester's skill - not black-box techniques, which are systematic and derived from the specification. Statements A, B, and C are all accurate syllabus statements.

option_notes.A: True - not the answer.
option_notes.B: True - not the answer.
option_notes.C: True - not the answer.
option_notes.D: Correct answer - this dependency-on-skill statement belongs to experience-based techniques, not black-box techniques.

questions.distractor_note: This mixes up which technique category the 'depends heavily on tester skill' property applies to - a classic exam move: take a true statement and reattach it to the wrong technique category.
questions.alt_wording: May ask directly: 'which technique category's effectiveness depends heavily on the tester's skill?' (experience-based).

questions.question: A car-insurance premium calculator classifies driver age into bands: Young (18-24), Standard (25-64), Senior (65 and above). Ages below 18 are rejected as invalid. Using Equivalence Partitioning, what is the MINIMUM number of test cases needed to achieve 100% partition coverage?
questions.why_correct: There are 4 partitions: 3 valid (Young, Standard, Senior) and 1 invalid (below 18). EP coverage requires exercising each identified partition, including invalid ones, at least once; one test value per partition suffices, so the minimum is 4 test cases (e.g., 20, 40, 70, 15).

option_notes.A: Incorrect - undercounts; only 2 of the 4 partitions would be exercised.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - covers only the 3 valid partitions, omitting the invalid (below-18) partition needed for 100% coverage.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - overcounts; testing both boundaries of each range would be Boundary Value Analysis, not EP, which needs only one value per partition.

questions.distractor_note: Option D reflects a common EP/BVA mix-up - EP's claim is that one representative value per partition is sufficient, not that every boundary must be tested.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to list the partitions themselves, or give the minimum test values directly, without asking for a numeric count.

questions.question: A warehouse system should trigger a reorder alert when stockLevel <= 50 units (i.e., 50 or fewer triggers a reorder). A developer accidentally implements this as 'if (stockLevel == 50) triggerReorder()' - only exactly 50, not the whole <=50 range. A tester derives 2-value BVA test data for this boundary: {50, 51}. Both tests pass their expected-vs-actual comparison despite the bug. Why did 2-value BVA fail to catch this defect, and what would catch it?

options.A: 2-value BVA is fundamentally unreliable and should be replaced entirely by exploratory testing
options.B: The defect requires white-box branch coverage, since equality bugs cannot be found by black-box techniques
options.C: 2-value BVA only exercises the boundary (50, correctly triggers under the bug) and its neighbor just outside the valid range (51, correctly does not trigger under the bug); 3-value BVA would add the neighbor just inside the valid range (49), which SHOULD trigger per spec but wouldn't under the buggy '==' check, exposing the defect
options.D: The defect cannot be found by any black-box technique because it is a coding-level mistake

questions.why_correct: This mirrors the syllabus's own worked example: for a boundary 'x <= 10' buggy-implemented as 'x = 10', 2-value BVA test data {10, 11} both accidentally pass under the bug, but 3-value BVA data {9, 10, 11} adds 9, which exposes the defect since the buggy code incorrectly rejects it. Here, 49 is the value that should trigger a reorder (49 <= 50) but wouldn't under the '==' bug, exposing the mismatch between expected and actual results.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - overreaching conclusion; 2-value BVA is a valid, useful technique, it simply has lower fault-detection power than 3-value BVA for this specific defect pattern.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - BVA is precisely applicable to this ordered numeric boundary; white-box coverage is a different (structure-based) technique category and isn't required to catch this.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - this is exactly the kind of coding-level boundary defect black-box BVA is designed to expose from the outside, without knowledge of the implementation.

questions.distractor_note: Both 2-value BVA tests (50 and 51) happen to produce correct-looking results under the bug, which is what makes this defect sneaky; only testing the neighbor on the OTHER side of the boundary (49, added by 3-value BVA) exposes the mismatch.
questions.alt_wording: May give you the buggy condition directly (e.g., 'if (x = 10)' instead of 'if (x <= 10)') and ask which BVA variant, or which specific input value, would detect the defect.

questions.question: A loan-approval system's decision table has three Boolean conditions (Credit score above threshold, Income verified, Existing default on record), giving a full table of 8 combinations. Two combinations are infeasible in the business domain (a default on record can never coincide with unverified income, per company policy) and are removed. Test cases exercise all remaining feasible columns. What is the decision table coverage achieved, and how many test cases were needed?

options.A: 75% coverage, 6 test cases
options.B: 100% coverage, 6 test cases
options.C: 100% coverage, 8 test cases
options.D: 75% coverage, 8 test cases

questions.why_correct: With 2 of the 8 full combinations removed as infeasible, 6 feasible columns remain. The coverage items in decision table testing are the feasible columns, so exercising all 6 gives 100% coverage (6/6), requiring 6 test cases.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - since ALL feasible columns (6 of 6) were exercised, coverage is 100%, not 75%.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - only 6 test cases are needed since infeasible combinations are removed, not the full 8.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - both parts are wrong; coverage is 100% with 6 test cases, not 75% with 8.

questions.distractor_note: This tempts you to divide exercised columns by the ORIGINAL 8-combination count instead of the reduced feasible-column count, but decision table coverage is defined relative to feasible columns only.
questions.alt_wording: May instead give the infeasible-combination count and ask how many feasible columns or test cases remain, without stating the coverage percentage achieved.

questions.topic: State Transition Testing - Coverage Criteria Comparison
questions.question: A ride-sharing trip has 4 states: Requested, DriverAssigned, InProgress, Completed, with valid transitions Requested->DriverAssigned (assign), DriverAssigned->InProgress (start), InProgress->Completed (finish), and DriverAssigned->Requested (driverCancels). A test lead wants 100% all transitions coverage for this safety-relevant flow. Which of the following test approaches achieves that?

options.A: A single test case that visits all 4 states in one pass: Requested -> DriverAssigned -> InProgress -> Completed
options.B: Test cases exercising all 4 valid transitions, plus attempts at invalid transitions shown in the state table (e.g., attempting Requested->InProgress or Completed->DriverAssigned directly), using no more than one invalid transition per test case
options.C: Test cases exercising only the 4 valid transitions, since invalid transitions are out of scope for state transition testing
options.D: A single test case attempting every invalid transition in one continuous run, to save execution time

questions.why_correct: All transitions coverage requires exercising all valid transitions and attempting the invalid transitions shown in a state table. The syllabus recommends testing only one invalid transition per test case to avoid defect masking, and full all transitions coverage is stated to be a minimum requirement for mission and safety-critical software.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - this only achieves all states coverage, and even misses full valid transitions coverage since it never exercises driverCancels; it does not achieve all transitions coverage.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - this describes valid transitions (0-switch) coverage, a weaker criterion than all transitions coverage, which the syllabus explicitly says must ALSO attempt invalid transitions.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the syllabus specifically warns against bundling multiple invalid transitions into a single test case, since it risks defect masking, where one defect prevents the detection of another; only one invalid transition per test case is recommended.

questions.distractor_note: Option A is tempting because visiting every state feels 'complete,' but all states coverage is explicitly the WEAKEST of the three criteria and doesn't guarantee every transition, like driverCancels, was exercised.
questions.alt_wording: May ask which coverage criterion is guaranteed by achieving another (e.g., achieving all transitions coverage guarantees both all states coverage and valid transitions coverage).

questions.question: A dosage-calculation function contains 15 executable statements. A test suite exercises 12 of them, including the line 'dosePerKg = totalDose / patientWeight' but never with patientWeight equal to zero. What is the statement coverage achieved, and would 100% statement coverage guarantee the division-by-zero defect is found?

options.A: 80% coverage; yes, reaching the statement is sufficient to guarantee any defect there is found
options.B: 80% coverage; no - reaching a statement doesn't guarantee it was exercised with the specific data (like patientWeight = 0) needed to trigger a data-dependent defect
options.C: 20% coverage; no, since coverage measures branches, not statements
options.D: 100% coverage; the function has no data-dependent defects by definition

questions.why_correct: Statement coverage = 12/15 = 80%. The syllabus explicitly warns that exercising a statement with a test case will not detect all defects - for example, a division by zero that only fails when the denominator is zero - since that is a data-dependent defect, not merely a matter of reaching the line.

option_notes.A: Incorrect on the guarantee claim - the 80% coverage figure is correct, but 100% coverage still wouldn't guarantee this specific defect is found, since it depends on the data used, not just whether the line executed.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - wrong percentage (12/15 = 80%, not 20%) and wrong description of what statement coverage measures.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - wrong percentage, and the claim about 'no data-dependent defects by definition' is not something a coverage percentage can determine.

questions.distractor_note: Option A gets the arithmetic right but then makes the classic false claim that reaching a statement is the same as exercising all the meaningful data conditions within it - the syllabus explicitly contradicts this with the division-by-zero example.
questions.alt_wording: May ask only for the coverage percentage as a pure calculation, or ask only about the data-dependency limitation without the arithmetic.

questions.question: A shopping-cart discount function has 8 branches (arising from several if/else statements and a switch/case for coupon types). A test suite executes 5 of them. What is the branch coverage, and does it also guarantee 100% statement coverage was achieved?

options.A: 62.5% branch coverage; no information about statement coverage can be inferred from this alone
options.B: 62.5% branch coverage; yes, achieving any branch coverage percentage always implies the identical statement coverage percentage
options.C: 37.5% branch coverage; the two measures are unrelated
options.D: 62.5% branch coverage; 100% statement coverage is guaranteed regardless of the branch coverage percentage achieved

questions.why_correct: Branch coverage = 5/8 = 62.5%. Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage only at the 100% level - 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage, but not vice versa. At a partial (62.5%) branch coverage figure, nothing specific can be concluded about the exact statement coverage percentage.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - branch and statement coverage are measured over different item counts (branches vs. statements) and don't move in lockstep; only the FULL (100%) branch-coverage case is guaranteed to imply full statement coverage.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - wrong percentage (5/8 = 62.5%, not 37.5%); also the two measures are related (branch coverage subsumes statement coverage at 100%), not unrelated.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - 100% statement coverage is not guaranteed at less than 100% branch coverage; the subsumption relationship only holds when branch coverage is fully at 100%.

questions.distractor_note: Option D exploits the true fact that '100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage' but misapplies it to a partial (62.5%) branch coverage figure, where no such guarantee exists.
questions.alt_wording: May instead give you both statement and branch coverage numbers and ask whether they are mutually consistent with a valid test suite.

questions.topic: Value and Limits of White-Box Testing
questions.question: An LMS's grading requirement states that a 'curve adjustment' must be applied to final scores below the class average, but the developer never implements this curve-adjustment logic at all - the requirement was simply missed. The team achieves 100% branch coverage on the grading module. What BEST explains why white-box testing did not catch this missing feature?

options.A: 100% branch coverage claims are always inflated and cannot be trusted
options.B: White-box testing takes the entire existing implementation into account, but since no code exists for a requirement that was never implemented, there is nothing for coverage measures to exercise - this is a defect of omission that white-box testing cannot detect
options.C: Branch coverage only applies to user-interface code, not to backend grading logic
options.D: The team should have used state transition testing instead, which always finds missing requirements

questions.why_correct: A fundamental weakness shared by all white-box test techniques is that if the software does not implement one or more requirements, white-box testing may not detect the resulting defects of omission, since coverage measures are based on code that exists, not on what SHOULD exist per the specification.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - 100% branch coverage of the code that DOES exist is legitimately achievable; the issue is that coverage says nothing about code that was never written.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - branch coverage applies to any executable code, front-end or back-end; the missing-requirement issue isn't about which layer the code lives in.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - no test technique guarantees finding every missing feature, which would contradict the absence-of-defects fallacy; state transition testing is also a black-box technique that could plausibly help here, but 'always finds' is an overreaching, unsupported claim.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask for the general STRENGTH of white-box testing as a contrast (it takes the entire implementation into account, helping detect defects even when the specification is vague or outdated).

questions.question: A tester recalls that hotel-booking apps have previously failed when a guest selects a check-out date earlier than the check-in date, and designs a specific test for that exact input combination even though it isn't called out anywhere in the current requirements. Which technique is being used?

options.A: Checklist-based testing
options.B: Error guessing
options.C: Decision table testing
options.D: State transition testing

questions.why_correct: Error guessing anticipates errors, defects, and failures based on the tester's knowledge, including how the application - or similar applications - has failed in the past, exactly matching this scenario.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - no checklist of general questions or conditions is being worked through; this is a targeted guess based on past failure knowledge.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - no table of condition/action combinations is described.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - no states, events, or transitions model is described.

questions.alt_wording: May instead describe this as a 'fault attack' targeting a known category of date-logic errors, built from a list of possible errors, defects, and failures.

questions.question: For a newly built mobile game level, one tester works through a checklist item by item ('Does the pause menu work?', 'Are all achievements unlockable?'), checking each independently. A different tester instead spends a one-hour timeboxed session freely exploring the level, guided by a test charter, designing and running new tests on the fly as they learn how the level behaves. How do these two approaches differ?

options.A: They don't differ; both are the same technique under different names
options.B: The first is checklist-based testing (test conditions from a checklist, checked independently); the second is exploratory testing (simultaneous test design, execution, and learning within a session, often structured with test charters and time boxes)
options.C: The first is exploratory testing; the second is checklist-based testing
options.D: Both are white-box techniques, since both require examining the game's internal code

questions.why_correct: Checklist-based testing uses a checklist of test conditions that can be checked independently and directly. Exploratory testing simultaneously designs, executes, and evaluates tests while learning about the test object, often structured with test charters within a time box, as described for the second tester.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - they are two distinct experience-based techniques with different structures.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - reversed.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - both are experience-based techniques, not white-box; neither requires examining internal code.

questions.distractor_note: Both techniques are experience-based, which can make them feel similar, but the checklist provides pre-defined items to verify, while exploratory testing's defining trait is designing tests IN THE MOMENT as understanding develops.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which technique is 'useful when specifications are inadequate or there is significant time pressure' (exploratory testing) or which 'should not contain items better suited as entry/exit criteria' (checklist-based testing).

questions.question: In the INVEST mnemonic for good user stories, what does the 'T' stand for, and why does it matter to testers?

options.A: Testable - if a stakeholder doesn't know how to test a user story, it may indicate the story isn't clear enough, doesn't reflect something valuable, or the stakeholder just needs help testing it
options.B: Timely - the story must be scheduled before any other stories in the backlog
options.C: Traceable - the story must be linked to a specific regulatory requirement
options.D: Trivial - the story must be simple enough to complete within a single day

questions.why_correct: INVEST stands for Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. The syllabus explicitly links the 'Testable' property to the idea that if a stakeholder doesn't know how to test a story, it may mean the story isn't clear, doesn't reflect value, or the stakeholder needs help.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - 'Timely' is not one of the INVEST letters, and no such scheduling rule is stated.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - 'Traceable' is not one of the INVEST letters, and the syllabus doesn't tie INVEST to regulatory linkage.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - 'Trivial' is not an INVEST letter; 'Small' is, but 'small' doesn't require single-day completion, and it is a distinct letter.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to spell out all six INVEST letters, or to identify which letter is violated when a story is too large to estimate confidently (Small or Estimable).

questions.question: A team practicing ATDD for a new 'pause subscription' feature holds a specification workshop where the product owner, a developer, and a tester jointly analyze and refine the story's acceptance criteria, resolving an ambiguity about how refunds should be handled during a pause. What should happen NEXT, per the syllabus's typical ATDD flow?

options.A: The team creates test cases based on the acceptance criteria, typically starting with positive cases, then negative cases, then relevant non-functional characteristics
options.B: The developer immediately writes all production code, then testers write test cases afterward to check it
options.C: The team skips test case creation entirely and relies only on the specification workshop notes
options.D: The team performs a full regression test suite run before any test cases for this story exist

questions.why_correct: After the specification workshop resolves ambiguity, the next ATDD step is creating test cases based on the acceptance criteria, typically positive cases first, then negative cases, then non-functional characteristics, matching the syllabus's stated typical order.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - ATDD is a test-first approach; test cases are created BEFORE the story is implemented, not written afterward to check finished code.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - test case creation from the acceptance criteria is a defined, essential ATDD step, not something to skip.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - a full regression run isn't the next ATDD step after a specification workshop; it's unrelated to deriving new test cases for this specific story.

questions.alt_wording: May ask who typically participates in creating the initial ATDD test cases (customers/business representatives, developers, and testers) or what the test cases become once automated (executable requirements).

questions.topic: Tester's Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning
questions.question: During release planning, a Scrum team's tester participates in writing testable user stories and acceptance criteria, contributes to project and quality risk analyses, and estimates test effort associated with user stories. According to the syllabus, which planning activity is this?

options.A: Release planning - it looks ahead to the product release, refines the backlog, and serves as the basis for the test approach across all iterations
options.B: Iteration planning - it only concerns the current sprint's backlog and nothing beyond it
options.C: Test completion - it consolidates lessons learned at project milestones
options.D: Test monitoring - it compares actual progress against the plan

questions.why_correct: This matches the syllabus's description of release planning and the tester's contribution to it: looking ahead to the release, refining the product backlog, and serving as the basis for the test approach and plan across all iterations, with testers writing testable stories and acceptance criteria, participating in risk analyses, and estimating test effort.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - iteration planning instead concerns the iteration backlog specifically, involving detailed risk analysis of user stories, testability, breaking stories into tasks, and estimating testing tasks - a narrower, more detailed activity than what's described.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - test completion occurs at project milestones to consolidate experience and testware, unrelated to this planning activity.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - test monitoring is an ongoing progress-tracking activity, not this planning activity.

questions.alt_wording: May instead describe iteration-planning tasks (breaking user stories into testing tasks, detailed risk analysis of user stories) and ask you to identify that as iteration planning instead of release planning.

questions.question: A government IT department's historical data shows a development-to-test effort ratio of 7:3 for similar past projects. The new project's development effort is estimated at 1,400 person-days. Using estimation based on ratios, what is the estimated test effort?

options.A: 400 person-days
options.B: 600 person-days
options.C: 980 person-days
options.D: 3,267 person-days

questions.why_correct: A development-to-test ratio of 7:3 means test effort is 3/7 of development effort. 1,400 x 3/7 = 600 person-days.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - this doesn't correspond to the 3/7 fraction of 1,400.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - this applies 0.7 (misreading the ratio as a percentage) rather than the 3:7 ratio fraction.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - this multiplies by 7/3 instead of 3/7, inverting the ratio.

questions.distractor_note: Ratio-based estimation questions are easy to invert under time pressure - always check which side of the ratio (development or test) the known number belongs to before dividing.
questions.alt_wording: May phrase the ratio as 'for every 7 days of development effort, 3 days of test effort were historically needed' or give the test effort and ask for development effort instead.

questions.topic: Test Pyramid - Layer Naming and Granularity
questions.question: One team names its test pyramid layers 'unit tests,' 'service tests,' and 'UI tests' (the original Cohn model); another team instead names its layers 'component tests,' 'component integration tests,' and 'end-to-end tests.' According to the syllabus, how should these two naming schemes be understood?

options.A: They represent two fundamentally incompatible models; only one can be considered ISTQB-correct
options.B: The syllabus explicitly allows the number and naming of pyramid layers to differ between models, as long as the underlying granularity/isolation/execution-time relationship between lower and higher layers still holds
options.C: The second naming scheme is a white-box technique, while the first is black-box
options.D: Layer naming is irrelevant, since the test pyramid does not actually relate to test automation decisions

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly states the number and naming of test pyramid layers may differ, citing both the original three-layer Cohn model (unit/service/UI tests) and another popular model (unit/integration/end-to-end tests) as valid examples, while the general relationship (higher layers = lower granularity, lower isolation, higher execution time) still applies.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - the syllabus explicitly presents both naming schemes as valid, non-conflicting examples of the same underlying model.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - neither naming scheme is inherently black-box or white-box; the test pyramid is about granularity and automation layering, not test technique category.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the syllabus explicitly says the test pyramid supports the team in test automation and test effort allocation decisions.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which characteristic increases as you move UP the pyramid (execution time) or decreases (granularity, isolation).

questions.question: A manufacturing plant's control software has two identified product risks assessed qualitatively on a risk matrix with three levels (Low, Medium, High) for both likelihood and impact. Risk A is rated Medium likelihood / High impact. Risk B is rated High likelihood / Medium impact. Using the syllabus's definition of risk level as a combination of likelihood and impact, which statement is correct?

options.A: Risk A automatically has a higher risk level than Risk B, because impact always outweighs likelihood
options.B: Risk B automatically has a higher risk level than Risk A, because likelihood always outweighs impact
options.C: Both risks combine one Medium and one High rating, so a qualitative risk matrix would typically place them at the same or a comparably high combined risk level, warranting comparable test attention
options.D: Risk level cannot be assessed qualitatively; only quantitative multiplication is valid per the syllabus

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states risk level combines risk likelihood and risk impact, and can be assessed using a quantitative approach (multiplication) or a qualitative approach using a risk matrix. Neither factor is stated to always outweigh the other; a matrix approach would typically map a Medium/High combination and a High/Medium combination to a comparable overall risk level, not one automatically dominating the other.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - the syllabus does not state impact always outweighs likelihood; risk level is a combination of both factors.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - likewise, likelihood does not always outweigh impact.
option_notes.C: Correct.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the syllabus explicitly allows a qualitative approach using a risk matrix, in addition to or instead of quantitative multiplication.

questions.distractor_note: Options A and B each assume one risk attribute categorically dominates the other - a tempting simplification, but the syllabus treats likelihood and impact as jointly determining risk level, without a fixed hierarchy between them.
questions.alt_wording: May instead give a quantitative pair (e.g., likelihood 0.5/impact 6 vs. likelihood 0.3/impact 8) and ask you to multiply and compare directly.

questions.topic: Product Risk Analysis and Test Scope
questions.question: Product risk analysis for an aviation maintenance-logging system flags 'incorrect logging of a completed safety inspection' as a high-likelihood, high-impact product risk. Which of the following BEST reflects how this finding should influence the test approach, per the syllabus?

options.A: It should have no effect on the test approach, since all requirements must be tested equally regardless of risk
options.B: It should influence the test scope, test levels/types performed, the test techniques and coverage applied, effort estimates, and prioritization toward more thorough testing of this area
options.C: It should only affect the budget, not any technical decisions about how testing is performed
options.D: It should be handled exclusively through risk transfer (e.g., insurance), with no additional testing required

questions.why_correct: This matches the syllabus's list of how product risk analysis results are used: determining test scope, test levels/types, test techniques/coverage, effort estimates, and prioritization to find critical defects early - all pointing toward more thorough treatment of high-risk areas.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - risk-based testing deliberately allocates MORE effort and rigor to higher-risk areas; treating all requirements equally defeats this purpose.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - the syllabus explicitly ties risk analysis results to technical decisions (scope, levels, types, techniques, coverage), not just budget.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - risk transfer is one general risk response option among several (mitigation by testing, acceptance, transfer, contingency plan), not the exclusive or mandatory response, and testing-based mitigation is explicitly listed as an available option.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which SPECIFIC testing-based mitigation actions apply here (e.g., selecting testers with the right skills, applying independence, appropriate test techniques and coverage).

questions.question: Beyond mitigating a risk through testing, which of the following is one of the general response options to an analyzed product risk that the syllabus describes?

options.A: Risk acceptance - proceeding without further action because the risk is judged tolerable
options.B: Risk elimination - a guarantee that the risk can never occur again
options.C: Risk multiplication - recalculating likelihood and impact until the risk level reaches zero
options.D: Risk automation - replacing all human decision-making about the risk with a tool

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists several general response options to an analyzed risk: risk mitigation by testing, risk acceptance, risk transfer, or a contingency plan. Risk acceptance - doing nothing further because the risk is deemed tolerable - is one of these.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - no such concept as a guaranteed 'risk elimination' is described; testing cannot guarantee a risk will never occur, echoing the absence-of-defects fallacy.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - not a real risk-response concept in the syllabus; risk level isn't 'recalculated to zero.'
option_notes.D: Incorrect - not one of the listed response options; automation is a tooling topic (chapter 6), unrelated to this risk-response list.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to name all four response options (mitigation by testing, acceptance, transfer, contingency plan) or describe risk transfer via an example (e.g., purchasing insurance, outsourcing to a third party).

questions.question: 'Defect density' and 'number of defects found/fixed' belong to which category of test metric, and how does that differ from 'requirements coverage' and 'code coverage'?

options.A: Both pairs are defect metrics; there is no separate coverage-metrics category
options.B: 'Defect density'/'defects found/fixed' are defect metrics; 'requirements coverage'/'code coverage' are coverage metrics - a distinct category
options.C: 'Defect density'/'defects found/fixed' are coverage metrics; 'requirements coverage'/'code coverage' are defect metrics
options.D: Both pairs are cost metrics, since defects and coverage gaps both have a cost impact

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists defect metrics (e.g., number/priority of defects found/fixed, defect density, defect detection percentage) and coverage metrics (e.g., requirements coverage, code coverage) as two distinct categories among the common test metrics.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - coverage metrics are explicitly a separate, named category.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - reversed.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - cost metrics are yet another distinct category (e.g., cost of testing, organizational cost of quality), matching neither example pair given.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to classify 'residual risk level' (risk metric) or 'test environment preparation progress' (test progress metric) among the metric categories.

questions.question: A project has just finished its final system-test cycle before release. The team gathers data showing: which planned tests were executed, the achieved requirements coverage against the original test plan's exit criteria, deviations from the planned schedule, unresolved defects, and lessons learned for future projects. This report is generated once, at the end of the activity, rather than on a regular recurring basis. Which document is being described, and how does it differ from the document the team would have used DURING the test cycle to keep stakeholders informed of ongoing status?

options.A: This is a test completion report, prepared once at completion using progress-report data and other information, summarizing results against the original test plan; a test progress report, by contrast, is generated regularly (e.g., daily or weekly) during the activity to support ongoing test control
options.B: This is a defect report, and it differs from a risk register, which lists risks with likelihood and impact
options.C: This is a test plan, and it differs from a test charter used in exploratory testing sessions
options.D: This is a confirmation testing record, and it differs from a regression testing log

questions.why_correct: A test completion report is prepared during test completion, once an activity such as a test level or test cycle is complete, using test progress reports and other data, summarizing results against the original test plan (objectives, exit criteria), deviations, unresolved defects, and lessons learned. A test progress report, by contrast, is generated regularly during the activity (e.g., daily or weekly) to support ongoing test control - exactly the 'once at completion' vs. 'regularly during' distinction asked about.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - a defect report documents a single anomaly for triage and tracking; it doesn't match the 'summarize the whole cycle's results, once, at completion' description, and a risk register is a test-planning work product, not the ongoing-status document being contrasted here.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - a test plan is created during planning, before execution, to define objectives, approach, and schedule, not a document summarizing what already happened; a test charter guides an exploratory session, unrelated to this scenario.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - confirmation and regression testing are dynamic-testing activities performed after a fix, not documents or reports, and neither matches 'summarizes an entire completed test cycle' or 'regular ongoing status' descriptions.

questions.distractor_note: This question borrows recognizable pieces from several chapter-5 topics (defect reports, risk registers, test plans, confirmation/regression testing) as distractors to check whether you can isolate which concept the scenario is actually describing - test completion vs. test progress reporting - rather than just recognizing familiar vocabulary.
questions.alt_wording: May ask which report 'uses test progress reports and other data as input' (test completion report) or which document ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3 calls a 'test status report' (the progress report).

questions.question: An automotive firmware team needs to prove, for an audit, exactly which version of the test environment, test cases, and test scripts were used to produce a specific set of test results from three months ago, and needs the ability to restore that exact combination if a dispute arises. Which practice makes this possible?

options.A: Risk-based testing, since risk registers are versioned
options.B: Configuration management, which uniquely identifies, version-controls, and tracks changes to configuration items, and allows reverting to a previous baseline
options.C: Test case prioritization, since it orders execution by risk
options.D: Checklist-based testing, since checklists are regularly updated

questions.why_correct: Configuration management (CM) provides a discipline for identifying, controlling, and tracking work products such as test plans, test cases, test scripts, test results, and test logs as configuration items. It keeps a record of changed items when a new baseline is created and allows reverting to a previous baseline to reproduce previous test results - exactly what this audit requires.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - risk-based testing concerns prioritizing test effort by risk, not version-controlling test artifacts.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - test case prioritization concerns execution order, not artifact versioning or audit trails.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - checklist-based testing is an experience-based test design technique, unrelated to configuration tracking.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask how CM ensures 'traceability can be maintained throughout the test process' or how it 'unambiguously references all identified documentation and software items.'

questions.question: According to the syllabus, which of the following best describes what configuration management (CM) ensures to properly support testing?

options.A: All configuration items, including test items, are uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes, and related to other configuration items so that traceability can be maintained throughout the test process
options.B: CM guarantees that all defects are fixed before a baseline is created
options.C: CM replaces the need for a defect management process
options.D: CM is only relevant to hardware projects, not software test artifacts

questions.why_correct: This is close to the syllabus's own wording describing what CM ensures to support testing: unique identification, version control, change tracking, and relationships between configuration items for traceability.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - CM manages versions and baselines of configuration items; it doesn't guarantee defect-free baselines, which would contradict the absence-of-defects fallacy.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - defect management (section 5.5) is a separate, distinct process from configuration management (section 5.4).
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the syllabus discusses CM explicitly for software test work products, such as test plans, test cases, test scripts, test results, and logs.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask what happens when a configuration item is 'approved for testing' (it becomes a baseline, changeable only through formal change control).

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a defect found in an airline check-in system:

I. A defect report logged during dynamic testing should include the test object and test environment identification, and the context in which the defect was found (e.g., the test case or activity being performed).
II. Severity (degree of impact) and priority (urgency to fix) are considered the same attribute and should not both appear on a defect report.
III. Defect report status values such as 'open,' 'deferred,' 'awaiting confirmation testing,' and 'closed' are typical, as described by the syllabus.

Which statements are correct?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and III only
options.D: I, II, and III

questions.why_correct: Statements I and III both match the syllabus's list of typical defect report content: test object/environment identification, context, and status values like open, deferred, awaiting confirmation testing, and closed, among others. Statement II is false - severity and priority are explicitly listed as two SEPARATE fields (degree of impact vs. urgency to fix), not the same attribute.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - II is false.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - I is true, so this combination is wrong.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - II is false.

questions.distractor_note: Severity and priority are commonly confused in practice - a defect can be high severity (crashes the app) but low priority (affects a rarely-used feature), or vice versa (low severity but high priority for cosmetic branding reasons on a high-visibility page). The syllabus lists them as two distinct fields.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to distinguish severity from priority directly with a scenario where they diverge (e.g., a rarely used but crash-causing bug vs. a highly visible but harmless cosmetic bug).

questions.question: A tester observes that tapping 'Download for Offline' on a streaming app produces no error but silently fails to download the episode. Which defect report title BEST follows good defect-reporting practice?

options.A: 'Download for Offline silently fails for a selected episode with no error message shown to the user, on [device/OS version]'
options.B: 'Downloads are broken'
options.C: 'Whoever built the offline feature clearly didn't test it'
options.D: 'Urgent: fix this now or we lose subscribers'

questions.why_correct: A good defect report should provide sufficient, objective information to enable reproduction and resolution. Option A specifies the exact action, the observed (lack of) behavior, and context (device/OS), matching the syllabus's description of defect report content and objectives.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - too vague to guide reproduction, triage, or resolution; doesn't specify which action, feature area, or conditions.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - blames an individual rather than objectively describing the observed behavior; unhelpful and unprofessional.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - expresses urgency and opinion instead of objective information; severity and priority should be captured as their own structured fields, not asserted rhetorically in the title.

questions.alt_wording: May ask you to identify what's MISSING from a given defect report (e.g., no expected vs. actual result, no environment information, no reproduction steps) rather than compare full report titles.

questions.topic: Tool Support for Testing - Tool Type Comparison
questions.question: A team uses one tool to generate test data and test procedures during test design, and a separate tool to run automated tests and measure code coverage during test execution. How does the syllabus classify these two tool types?

options.A: Both are the same tool type; 'test design' and 'test execution' are not meaningfully distinguished in tool support
options.B: The first is a test design and test implementation tool (facilitates generation of test cases, test data, and test procedures); the second is a test execution and test coverage tool (facilitates automated test execution and coverage measurement)
options.C: The first is a static testing tool; the second is a DevOps tool
options.D: The first is a non-functional testing tool; the second is a collaboration tool

questions.why_correct: This matches the syllabus's tool-type list directly: test design and test implementation tools facilitate generation of test cases, test data, and test procedures; test execution and test coverage tools facilitate automated test execution and coverage measurement.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - the syllabus explicitly lists these as separate, named tool types among several categories.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - static testing tools support reviews and static analysis with no execution involved; DevOps tools support the delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, and CI/CD - neither matches the descriptions given.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - non-functional testing tools support hard-or-impossible-to-do-manually non-functional testing, such as load simulation; collaboration tools facilitate communication - neither matches the descriptions given.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which tool type 'increases test process efficiency by facilitating management of the SDLC, requirements, tests, defects, configuration' (test management tools).

questions.topic: Test Objectives - Verifying Requirements vs Validating Stakeholder Expectations
questions.question: A smart-home company's QA team performs two separate activities on a new thermostat-scheduling feature: (1) confirming that the feature does exactly what the written specification says a scheduling rule should do, and (2) separately checking, with actual homeowners, whether the scheduling feature behaves the way real users expect and actually solves their day-to-day comfort problem. Which two test objectives are these activities primarily pursuing, respectively?

options.A: Verifying whether specified requirements have been fulfilled, then validating whether the test object is complete and works as expected by the stakeholders
options.B: Building confidence in the quality of the test object, then ensuring required coverage of the test object
options.C: Reducing the risk level of inadequate software quality, then verifying compliance with contractual, legal, and regulatory requirements
options.D: Both activities pursue the same test objective, since they both involve the thermostat-scheduling feature

questions.why_correct: The first activity - checking behavior against the written specification - matches the test objective 'verifying whether specified requirements have been fulfilled.' The second - checking with real users whether the feature meets their actual needs - matches 'validating whether the test object is complete and works as expected by the stakeholders.' These are two distinct, named test objectives from the syllabus's list of nine.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - neither activity described is primarily about building general confidence or about coverage; they specifically target requirement conformance and stakeholder validation respectively.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - no contractual/legal/regulatory angle or general risk-reduction framing is described; the scenario is specifically about specification conformance versus real-user validation.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the two activities target different test objectives; checking against a written spec is a different objective than checking with real users, even though both concern the same feature.

questions.distractor_note: This mirrors the verification-vs-validation distinction from 1.1's concept notes, but phrased using the specific named test-objective wording (evaluating requirement fulfillment vs. validating stakeholder expectations) rather than the general 'verification/validation' terms, since the exam sometimes tests the specific nine-item objective list directly instead of the broader concept.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which single test objective from the list of nine is being pursued when only ONE of the two activities is described.

questions.topic: Quality Control - Other Approaches Beyond Testing
questions.question: Besides testing, which of the following does the syllabus name as another quality control approach used in software and systems engineering, alongside testing?

options.A: Formal methods (e.g., model checking and proof of correctness), simulation, and prototyping
options.B: Risk-based testing and confirmation testing
options.C: Test-driven development and behavior-driven development
options.D: Configuration management and defect management

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states testing is a major form of quality control, while other quality control approaches include formal methods (model checking and proof of correctness), simulation, and prototyping.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - risk-based testing and confirmation testing are both testing-related concepts, not alternative QC approaches to testing.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - TDD/BDD are test-first development approaches (chapter 2), not QC approaches named alongside testing in section 1.2.2.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - configuration management and defect management are test-management support practices (chapter 5), not alternative quality control approaches.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask what QA's relationship to the development process is, not just testing (QA applies to both development and testing processes, and is the responsibility of everyone on the project).

questions.question: A utility company reviews the draft requirements for a new smart-meter billing calculation before any firmware code is written, and catches an ambiguity about how partial-month usage should be prorated. Fixing this ambiguity at the requirements stage, instead of after the firmware ships to millions of meters, illustrates which testing principle?

options.A: Early testing saves time and money
options.B: Tests wear out
options.C: Testing is context dependent
options.D: Absence-of-defects fallacy

questions.why_correct: The 'early testing saves time and money' principle states that defects removed early in the process will not cause subsequent defects in derived work products, and the cost of quality is reduced since fewer failures occur later in the SDLC; both static and dynamic testing should start as early as possible - exactly matching reviewing requirements before firmware is written.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - tests wearing out concerns repeated tests losing effectiveness over time, not the timing of defect discovery.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - context dependence is a true general principle but doesn't specifically explain the benefit of catching this defect early.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the absence-of-defects fallacy concerns verification passing without guaranteeing user success, unrelated to the timing benefit described here.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask what would happen if this ambiguity were caught only after firmware shipped to millions of meters (higher cost of quality, more failures later in the SDLC).

questions.topic: Testing Principles - Presence of Defects vs Absence-of-Defects Fallacy
questions.question:
Consider the following two statements about an online voting system that has passed every specified test case with zero defects remaining open:

I. This result proves the system is free of defects, since testing found none.
II. Even if this result is accurate, the system could still fail to meet voters' actual needs and expectations, since thoroughly testing all specified requirements does not guarantee the system fulfills stakeholders' actual needs.

Which is correct?

options.A: Only I is correct
options.B: Only II is correct
options.C: Both I and II are correct
options.D: Neither I nor II is correct

questions.why_correct: Statement I contradicts the first testing principle: testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects - even if no defects are found, testing cannot prove test object correctness. Statement II matches the absence-of-defects fallacy: thoroughly testing all specified requirements and fixing all found defects could still produce a system that does not fulfill users' needs and expectations.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - I is false.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - I is false.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - II is true.

questions.distractor_note: Statement I exploits a very natural but incorrect inference - 'zero defects found' sounds like 'zero defects exist' - but the syllabus explicitly names this exact reasoning error as a violation of the first principle, distinct from (though related to) the absence-of-defects fallacy in statement II, which is about a stronger claim (verification success guaranteeing overall system success).
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to name which specific principle each statement violates or matches, rather than judging true/false.

questions.question: Beyond evaluating coverage, which of the following additional benefits does the syllabus attribute to good traceability between the test basis and testware?

options.A: It makes it possible to determine the impact of changes, facilitates audits, and helps meet IT governance criteria
options.B: It automatically fixes defects found during test execution
options.C: It eliminates the need for a test completion report
options.D: It guarantees that all identified risks have been fully mitigated

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states that in addition to evaluating coverage, good traceability makes it possible to determine the impact of changes, facilitates audits, and helps meet IT governance criteria; it also makes test progress and completion reports more easily understandable and helps communicate technical aspects of testing to stakeholders.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - traceability supports information and visibility, but does not fix defects; that is debugging.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - traceability actually makes completion reports MORE understandable; it doesn't eliminate the need for them.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - traceability helps evaluate residual risk, but doesn't guarantee risks are 'fully mitigated,' which would echo the absence-of-defects fallacy.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask what traceability of test results to risks is used to evaluate (the level of residual risk in a test object).

questions.question: An aviation software company is deciding who should test a new flight-planning module. Option 1: the developer who wrote the module tests it themselves. Option 2: a peer developer on the same team tests it. Option 3: an internal test team from a different department in the same company tests it. Option 4: an external testing company, outside the organization entirely, tests it. According to the syllabus's classification of levels of test independence, how should these four options be ranked from LOWEST to HIGHEST independence?

options.A: Option 1 (no independence), Option 2 (some independence), Option 3 (high independence), Option 4 (very high independence)
options.B: Option 4 (no independence), Option 3 (some independence), Option 2 (high independence), Option 1 (very high independence)
options.C: All four options provide the same level of independence, since all are qualified to test the module
options.D: Option 2 (no independence), Option 1 (some independence), Option 4 (high independence), Option 3 (very high independence)

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states work products can be tested by their author (no independence), by the author's peers from the same team (some independence), by testers from outside the author's team but within the organization (high independence), or by testers from outside the organization (very high independence) - exactly matching Options 1 through 4 in order.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - completely reverses the ranking.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - the syllabus explicitly distinguishes four different levels of independence based on who performs the testing.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - options are shuffled into the wrong independence levels.

questions.distractor_note: It's easy to conflate 'high independence' with 'highest possible rigor' and assume any tester outside the immediate author counts as maximally independent - but the syllabus specifically separates 'outside the author's team but within the organization' (high) from 'outside the organization' (very high), a distinction test-takers often collapse into one category.
questions.alt_wording: May instead describe just two of the four options and ask which has greater independence, or ask what independence is NOT a replacement for (familiarity - e.g., developers can efficiently find many defects in their own code).

questions.topic: Good Testing Practices - Avoiding Redundancy Across Test Levels
questions.question: A telecom company's test strategy assigns component testing, system testing, and acceptance testing each a distinct set of objectives, so that no single defect type is expected to be caught redundantly by all three levels. According to the syllabus, which SDLC-independent good testing practice does this illustrate?

options.A: Different test levels have specific and different test objectives, which allows for testing to be appropriately comprehensive while avoiding redundancy
options.B: Test levels should always be executed in a strictly identical, unchangeable sequence in every SDLC
options.C: Every test level must use exactly the same test technique to remain consistent
options.D: Only the system testing level needs clearly defined objectives; other levels can share objectives freely

questions.why_correct: This is one of the syllabus's SDLC-independent good testing practices: different test levels have specific and different test objectives, which allows for testing to be appropriately comprehensive while avoiding redundancy.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - the syllabus notes test levels may overlap in time and this ordering may not apply in some iterative models.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - different levels commonly use different techniques suited to their objectives; uniformity of technique is not a stated good practice.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the practice applies to ALL test levels having distinct objectives, not just system testing.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask what problem arises if test levels are NOT distinguished by different objectives (redundant testing effort, or coverage gaps).

questions.question: A fintech team building a payment microservice follows a workflow where, for each small unit of functionality, a developer first writes a failing unit test, then writes just enough code to make it pass, then refactors both the test and the code. Separately, for the service's business-facing acceptance criteria, the team instead derives tests from those criteria as part of the system design process, before implementing the corresponding part of the application. Which test-first approaches are being described, respectively?

options.A: Test-Driven Development (TDD), then Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD)
options.B: Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD), then Test-Driven Development (TDD)
options.C: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD), then Test-Driven Development (TDD)
options.D: Both describe the same approach: Acceptance Test-Driven Development (ATDD)

questions.why_correct: TDD directs coding through test cases instead of extensive software design: tests are written first, code is written to satisfy the tests, and then both are refactored - matching the first description exactly. ATDD derives tests from acceptance criteria as part of the system design process, with tests written before the corresponding part of the application is developed - matching the second description exactly.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - reversed.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - the first description matches TDD, not BDD, since it centers on write-test/write-code/refactor for units of functionality, not natural-language Given/When/Then behavior specification.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the two workflows described are distinct approaches (TDD operates on small code units; ATDD operates on the acceptance criteria of the system design).

questions.distractor_note: BDD is a realistic distractor because it, too, is a test-first approach associated with acceptance-level behavior - but the described unit-level write-test/write-code/refactor loop is specifically TDD's hallmark, not BDD's natural-language Given/When/Then hallmark.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which approach is characterized by tests 'written in a simple form of natural language...usually using the Given/When/Then format' (BDD).

questions.question: Before go-live, a utility company's billing system undergoes a testing phase focused specifically on operational aspects: verifying backup and restore procedures, disaster recovery, and operator training materials, rather than verifying business functionality itself. Which form of acceptance testing does this MOST closely match?

options.A: User acceptance testing (UAT)
options.B: Operational acceptance testing
options.C: Alpha testing
options.D: Contractual acceptance testing

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists the main forms of acceptance testing as: user acceptance testing (UAT), operational acceptance testing, contractual acceptance testing, regulatory acceptance testing, alpha testing, and beta testing. Operational acceptance testing is the form focused on operational readiness of the system (e.g., backup/restore, disaster recovery, operator training), rather than business functionality itself.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - UAT focuses on whether the system fulfills the user's business needs and functionality, not backup/restore or operator training specifically.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - alpha testing is typically performed by potential or existing customers at the developing organization's site, focused on functionality, not this operational-readiness focus.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - contractual acceptance testing checks compliance against a contract's acceptance criteria, not operational readiness procedures specifically.

questions.distractor_note: UAT is the classic first guess for 'acceptance testing,' but the scenario deliberately avoids describing business functionality checks, focusing instead on operational concerns (backup, recovery, operator training) - exactly the syllabus's operational acceptance testing.
questions.alt_wording: May instead describe regulatory acceptance testing (checking compliance with applicable regulations) or beta testing (performed by potential/existing customers at their own site) and ask you to name the form.

questions.question: A tester for a video-conferencing app checks that screen-sharing starts successfully when the presenter clicks 'Share Screen.' The same tester then separately checks whether screen-sharing works correctly when the presenter is on Windows and other participants are on macOS and a web browser, simultaneously. Which statement BEST classifies these two checks?

options.A: Both checks are functional, since both concern the same screen-sharing feature
options.B: The first check is functional (does screen-sharing work at all); the second is non-functional, evaluating the compatibility quality characteristic (how well the feature behaves across a mixed set of platforms/environments)
options.C: The first check is non-functional because it depends on the UI; the second is functional because it produces a pass/fail outcome
options.D: Neither check is valid testing unless the underlying code is examined

questions.why_correct: Functional testing evaluates 'what' the system should do (does screen-sharing start). Non-functional testing evaluates 'how well' it behaves; compatibility is one of the ISO/IEC 25010 non-functional quality characteristics listed by the syllabus (alongside performance efficiency, usability, reliability, security, maintainability, portability, and safety), and cross-platform interoperability is a textbook compatibility concern.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - using the same feature for both checks doesn't make them the same test type; what's evaluated (presence of the behavior vs. its quality across environments) differs.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - depending on the UI doesn't make a check non-functional, and producing a pass/fail outcome doesn't make a check functional; both can produce pass/fail results.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - both are legitimate black-box dynamic tests requiring no code inspection.

questions.distractor_note: Option C misapplies plausible-sounding but irrelevant classification criteria (UI dependency, pass/fail format) instead of the correct WHAT-vs-HOW-WELL distinction.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to sort several checks (app opens, app opens within 2 seconds, app works on both iOS and Android, error text is readable) into functional vs. non-functional buckets, using different ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics each time.

questions.question: A hospital is planning maintenance testing for a moderate change to its patient-record system. According to the syllabus, which factors typically determine the SCOPE of this maintenance testing?

options.A: The degree of risk of the change, the size of the existing system, and the size of the change
options.B: Only the number of developers available to implement the change
options.C: Only whether the change is a hot fix or a planned enhancement
options.D: The system's original purchase price and vendor contract length

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states the scope of maintenance testing typically depends on the degree of risk of the change, the size of the existing system, and the size of the change.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - developer headcount is a resourcing concern, not a stated scope factor.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - hot fix vs. planned enhancement is a maintenance TRIGGER classification, not a stated scope factor.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - purchase price and contract length are not stated scope factors for maintenance testing.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask which maintenance TRIGGER category (modification, environment upgrade/migration, or retirement) applies to a given scenario, rather than asking about scope factors.

questions.topic: Static Testing Value and Early Testing Principle (Mixed)
questions.question: During a review of a telecom API's interface specification document, a reviewer notices that one endpoint's specification lists a parameter as an integer, while the corresponding client library documentation expects a string for the same parameter - a mismatch that would only be discovered through an integration test failure if it weren't caught now. Considering both the static-testing chapter and the testing-principles chapter of the syllabus, which pair of statements BEST explains why this review is valuable?

options.A: It exemplifies static testing finding a typical defect type - incorrect interface specifications - that is easier and cheaper to find statically, AND it exemplifies the 'early testing saves time and money' principle, since catching this before integration testing avoids a costlier failure later
options.B: It exemplifies dynamic testing triggering a failure, AND it exemplifies the 'tests wear out' principle
options.C: It exemplifies the absence-of-defects fallacy, AND it exemplifies debugging rather than testing
options.D: It exemplifies exploratory testing, AND it exemplifies the 'defects cluster together' principle

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly lists 'incorrect interface specifications (e.g., mismatched number, type, or order of parameters)' among the typical defects that are easier and/or cheaper to find through static testing. It also matches the early testing principle: defects removed early (here, during a document review, before integration testing would have triggered a failure) reduce the cost of quality, since fewer failures occur later in the SDLC.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - no code was executed and no failure was triggered; this is static testing, which finds defects directly, not dynamic testing; and 'tests wear out' concerns repeated tests losing effectiveness, unrelated to this scenario.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - the absence-of-defects fallacy concerns verification not guaranteeing user success, and this is clearly testing (a review), not debugging (removing a known defect from code).
option_notes.D: Incorrect - no time-boxed, simultaneous-design-and-execution session is described (that would be exploratory testing), and no claim about defect concentration in a small number of components is made (that would be defect clustering).

questions.distractor_note: This question deliberately mixes vocabulary from chapter 3 (static testing defect types) and chapter 1 (testing principles) in the same options, so options B-D borrow real, correct-sounding terms from BOTH chapters but attach them to the wrong scenario details - only option A correctly uses BOTH concepts in a way that matches the scenario.
questions.alt_wording: May instead isolate just the static-testing defect-type angle or just the early-testing-principle angle as two separate, single-concept questions.

questions.topic: Review Roles - Manager vs Review Leader
questions.question: For a formal review of aerospace flight-control software, one stakeholder decides which specific documents will be reviewed this quarter and allocates staff time and budget for the review effort. A different stakeholder is then responsible for deciding exactly who will be involved in a specific review session and organizing when and where that session will take place. What are these two roles called, respectively?

options.A: Manager, then Review leader
options.B: Review leader, then Manager
options.C: Moderator, then Scribe
options.D: Author, then Reviewer

questions.why_correct: The Manager decides what is to be reviewed and provides resources, such as staff and time for the review. The Review leader takes overall responsibility for a specific review, such as deciding who will be involved, and organizing when and where the review will take place.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - reversed.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - the Moderator ensures the effective running of review meetings (mediation, time management, safe environment); the Scribe collates anomalies and records review information - neither description matches deciding what to review/allocating resources, or organizing who/when/where for a specific session.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - the Author creates and fixes the work product; the Reviewer performs reviews - neither matches these descriptions.

questions.distractor_note: Manager and Review leader are easy to conflate because both sound like 'the person in charge' - the key discriminator is scope: the Manager operates at the organizational/resourcing level (what gets reviewed, budget), while the Review leader operates at the level of a specific review session (who/when/where for that one review).
questions.alt_wording: May instead describe the Scribe or Moderator's responsibilities and ask you to distinguish them from Manager/Review leader, mixing all six principal review roles into a matching exercise.

questions.topic: Review Process Activities - Planning vs Review Initiation
questions.question: For a pharmaceutical company's review of a new standard operating procedure (SOP) document, one phase defines the purpose of the review, which quality characteristics will be evaluated, the exit criteria, and the effort and timeframe involved. A later, separate phase instead confirms that every participant has access to the SOP document, understands their assigned role, and has received everything needed to perform the review. Which two review-process activities are these, respectively?

options.A: Planning, then Review initiation
options.B: Review initiation, then Planning
options.C: Individual review, then Communication and analysis
options.D: Fixing and reporting, then Planning

questions.why_correct: Planning defines the scope of the review - purpose, work product, quality characteristics to evaluate, areas to focus on, exit criteria, supporting information, effort, and timeframes. Review initiation follows, ensuring everyone and everything involved is prepared to start: participants have access to the work product, understand their role and responsibilities, and have what they need to perform the review.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - reversed; planning defines scope/exit criteria before initiation confirms readiness to start.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - individual review is where reviewers privately assess the work product and log anomalies; communication and analysis is where the group discusses and decides on anomalies - neither matches defining review scope or confirming participant readiness.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - fixing and reporting happens after anomalies are identified and analyzed, not at the start of the process.

questions.distractor_note: Planning and Review initiation are easy to blur together since both happen 'before the real reviewing starts' - the discriminator is WHAT is being decided: Planning sets the review's scope and criteria; Review initiation confirms logistical readiness against a scope that's already been set.
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask you to sequence all five review-process activities (Planning, Review initiation, Individual review, Communication and analysis, Fixing and reporting) in order.

questions.topic: White-Box Testing Used Within Static Testing
questions.question: An automotive team performs a manual 'dry run' walkthrough of newly written ECU (engine control unit) code, tracing through its control-flow logic by reading the code and mentally executing it line by line, without compiling or running it on any hardware. The team uses knowledge of the code's branch structure to decide which paths to trace. Which statement BEST classifies this activity with respect to the test technique categories described in the syllabus?

options.A: This cannot be white-box testing, since no code was executed; only black-box testing can be performed without execution
options.B: This is white-box testing being applied within static testing - white-box test techniques are well suited to reviewing code not yet ready for execution, using knowledge of the code's structure (e.g., a control flow graph), even though no execution occurs
options.C: This is purely an experience-based technique, since it relies on the reviewer's general knowledge rather than a specification or structure
options.D: This activity cannot be classified under any of the three test technique categories, since it mixes review with technique knowledge

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly states that white-box test techniques can be used in static testing (e.g., during dry runs of code); they are well suited to reviewing code not yet ready for execution, pseudocode, and other high-level or top-down logic that can be modeled with a control flow graph. Using knowledge of the code's structure to guide a manual trace is exactly this.

option_notes.A: Incorrect - this exact scenario (a code dry run using structural knowledge, without execution) is the syllabus's own example of white-box testing applied statically.
option_notes.B: Correct.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - the activity is driven by the code's internal structure (branches, control flow), which is the defining trait of the white-box (structure-based) category, not tester experience/intuition alone.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - it fits cleanly into the white-box category; static vs. dynamic (does it execute?) and black-box vs. white-box vs. experience-based (what information source is used?) are two independent classification axes.

questions.distractor_note: The word 'static' strongly primes test-takers to think 'black-box, no structure involved' - but static/dynamic and black-box/white-box/experience-based are two independent classification axes; a technique can be structure-based (white-box) while never executing anything (static).
questions.alt_wording: May instead ask for a general strength of white-box testing (taking the entire implementation into account, helping detect defects even when the specification is vague, outdated, or incomplete).

questions.question: According to the syllabus, what is the relationship between experience-based test techniques and black-box/white-box test techniques?

options.A: Experience-based test techniques are complementary to black-box and white-box test techniques, and can detect defects that those technique categories may miss
options.B: Experience-based test techniques always replace the need for black-box and white-box techniques once a tester is sufficiently experienced
options.C: Experience-based test techniques are a subtype of white-box test techniques, since both require tester skill
options.D: Experience-based test techniques cannot be used together with black-box or white-box techniques in the same test effort

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states that experience-based test techniques can detect defects that may be missed using black-box and white-box test techniques, and are therefore complementary to those two categories.

option_notes.A: Correct.
option_notes.B: Incorrect - the syllabus frames experience-based techniques as complementary, not as a replacement for the other two categories.
option_notes.C: Incorrect - experience-based techniques are a distinct, third category, not a subtype of white-box techniques.
option_notes.D: Incorrect - nothing in the syllabus prevents combining technique categories within the same test effort; in fact exploratory testing can incorporate other technique categories such as equivalence partitioning.

questions.alt_wording: May instead ask what experience-based techniques' effectiveness depends heavily on (the tester's skill).
