This matches the final step described in the scenario exactly: defects have been fixed and verified, exit criteria are confirmed as met, the work product is accepted, and results are reported. The earlier review meeting, where anomalies were discussed and classified into defects versus false positives with owners assigned, is a separate, earlier activity called 'Communication and analysis' - the question asks specifically about what happens afterward, not about the meeting itself.

option_notes.A: This describes the earlier part of the scenario (the review meeting where anomalies are discussed, classified as defects or false positives, and assigned owners), not the final step the question asks about. It is tempting because the passage does mention a meeting, but the question specifically points to what happened two weeks later, after the meeting.
option_notes.B: Individual review happens even earlier than the meeting, when each reviewer works alone to examine the work product and log anomalies, recommendations, and questions. Nothing in the final step described (fixes verified, exit criteria met, acceptance, reporting) involves an individual, private examination.
option_notes.C: Correct. Creating defect reports for confirmed defects, reaching exit criteria, accepting the work product, and reporting the results is precisely the 'Fixing and reporting' activity as defined in the syllabus.
option_notes.D: Review initiation is the very first activity, occurring before any anomalies are even logged - it ensures every participant has access to the work product and understands their role. It has nothing to do with fixes, exit criteria, or final reporting, which all happen much later in the process.

questions.distractor_note: This question embeds two different review-process activities in one scenario: the meeting (Communication and analysis) and the later step (Fixing and reporting), but only asks about the second one. A reader who scans for the word 'meeting' or 'discussed anomalies' may reflexively pick Communication and analysis without noticing the question is really asking about the acceptance-and-reporting step that happened two weeks afterward.
questions.alt_wording: This could be asked as a sequencing question ('Put the following four review-process activities in the order they occur: Fixing and reporting, Individual review, Planning, Communication and analysis') or as a direct comparison question contrasting what happens during Communication and analysis versus what happens during Fixing and reporting.

questions.topic: Test Management Tools vs DevOps Tools
questions.question: A software company uses Tool X to track requirements, link them to test cases, log and manage defects, and produce SDLC-wide progress reports shared across several teams. It separately uses Tool Y to automatically trigger a build, run the CI/CD pipeline, and coordinate deployments whenever a developer commits code. According to the syllabus, which of the following correctly identifies Tool X and Tool Y?

options.A: Tool X is a DevOps tool; Tool Y is a test management tool
options.B: Tool X is a test management tool; Tool Y is a DevOps tool
options.C: Tool X is a test execution tool; Tool Y is a collaboration tool
options.D: Tool X is a static testing tool; Tool Y is a test design tool

questions.why_correct: The syllabus describes test management tools as tools that 'increase the test process efficiency by facilitating management of the SDLC, requirements, tests, defects, configuration' - which matches Tool X's job of tracking requirements, linking them to test cases, managing defects, and producing SDLC-wide reports. It describes DevOps tools as tools that 'support the DevOps delivery pipeline, workflow tracking, automated build process(es), CI/CD' - which matches Tool Y's job of triggering builds, running the CI/CD pipeline, and coordinating deployments on every commit.

option_notes.A: This reverses the correct mapping. Tool X's functions (requirements traceability, test and defect management, SDLC-wide reporting) are the definition of a test management tool, not a DevOps tool; Tool Y's functions (builds, CI/CD, deployment coordination) define a DevOps tool, not a test management tool.
option_notes.B: Correct - this matches each tool's described functions to the syllabus definition of its tool category.
option_notes.C: Test execution tools facilitate automated running of tests and coverage measurement, not requirement traceability or defect management, so it does not fit Tool X. Collaboration tools facilitate communication between people, not automated builds or CI/CD pipelines, so it does not fit Tool Y either.
option_notes.D: Static testing tools support reviews and static analysis, and test design tools facilitate generating test cases, test data, and test procedures - neither category matches Tool X's SDLC-wide requirement/defect management role or Tool Y's build-and-deployment automation role.

questions.distractor_note: Option A is the most tempting wrong answer because both 'DevOps tool' and 'test management tool' are genuine syllabus categories being tested here - the distractor simply swaps which tool gets which label, testing whether the reader maps the described behavior to the correct name rather than just recognizing the two category names.
questions.alt_wording: This could be asked as a negative question ('Which of the following is NOT a function associated with DevOps tools, according to the syllabus?') or as a direct-definition question ('What is the primary purpose of a test management tool, according to the syllabus?').

questions.question: A test lead is briefing a new hire and avoids the official ISTQB terms, instead saying: 'One category of technique looks only at what the system is specified to do, without ever looking at the code - if the implementation changes but the required behavior stays the same, the same tests are still useful. Another category looks at the code's internal structure and paths, and can only be used once the code exists.' Which official ISTQB terms correspond to these two descriptions, in order?

options.A: Black-box test techniques (also called specification-based techniques), and white-box test techniques (also called structure-based techniques)
options.B: White-box test techniques (also called specification-based techniques), and black-box test techniques (also called structure-based techniques)
options.C: Experience-based test techniques, and black-box test techniques
options.D: Black-box test techniques, and experience-based test techniques (also called structure-based techniques)

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states black-box test techniques are 'also known as specification-based techniques,' based on analyzing specified behavior without reference to internal structure - which is exactly why black-box test cases remain valid if the implementation changes but required behavior does not. White-box test techniques are 'also known as structure-based techniques,' based on analyzing the test object's internal structure and processing, and can only be created after the design or implementation exists. The test lead's two descriptions map directly onto black-box (first) and white-box (second).

option_notes.A: Correct. Matches the syllabus's alternate names exactly: black-box = specification-based, white-box = structure-based.
option_notes.B: Wrong - reverses the pairing. White-box techniques depend on internal structure/code, so they are structure-based, not specification-based; black-box techniques analyze specified behavior, so they are specification-based, not structure-based.
option_notes.C: Wrong. Experience-based test techniques are not called 'specification-based' - they rely on tester knowledge and experience rather than a formal specification or the code structure. The first description (behavior-only, implementation-independent) matches black-box, not experience-based.
option_notes.D: Wrong on both counts. The first description matches black-box (whose correct alternate name is specification-based), and the second description - internal structure and code-dependent - matches white-box, not experience-based; experience-based techniques are not described as 'structure-based' anywhere in the syllabus.

questions.alt_wording: Which pair of official synonyms correctly replaces 'black-box' and 'white-box' in the sentence: 'Black-box test techniques are also known as ___ techniques, while white-box test techniques are also known as ___ techniques'?

questions.question: A streaming app selects video quality based on measured bandwidth in Mbps using these partitions: Low (greater than 0 and less than 5 Mbps), Medium (5 up to but not including 15 Mbps), High (15 up to but not including 50 Mbps), Ultra (50 Mbps or more), and Invalid (0 Mbps or a negative reading, e.g. a sensor error). A test suite runs with bandwidth values of 2, 10, 30, and 100 Mbps. What equivalence partition coverage does this test suite achieve, and how many additional test cases are needed to reach 100% coverage?

options.A: 80% coverage (4 of 5 partitions exercised); 1 more test case is needed, using any Invalid-partition value such as 0 or -1
options.B: 100% coverage; no more test cases are needed
options.C: 75% coverage (3 of 4 partitions exercised); 1 more test case is needed
options.D: 80% coverage; 2 more test cases are needed, one for a negative reading and a separate one for exactly 0

questions.why_correct: There are 5 identified partitions in total: the 4 valid partitions (Low, Medium, High, Ultra) and 1 invalid partition (readings <= 0). The test suite's values of 2 (Low), 10 (Medium), 30 (High), and 100 (Ultra) exercise all 4 valid partitions but never exercise the Invalid partition. Coverage = partitions exercised / total partitions identified = 4/5 = 80%. Per the syllabus, 100% equivalence partitioning coverage requires exercising all identified partitions, including invalid ones - so a single additional test case with any value from the Invalid partition (0, -1, -50, etc.) is enough to reach 100%, since any value in that partition counts as exercising it.

option_notes.A: Correct. 4 of 5 total partitions are exercised (80%); the missing partition is the single Invalid partition, so exactly one more test case (any value <= 0) completes coverage.
option_notes.B: Wrong. This forgets that the Invalid partition (bandwidth <= 0) is also a partition that must be exercised for 100% coverage - the syllabus is explicit that invalid partitions count toward coverage just like valid ones. Only 4 of the 5 total partitions were tested.
option_notes.C: Wrong. This undercounts the total number of partitions as 4 (treating only valid partitions as 'real' partitions and ignoring the Invalid partition entirely), which produces both an incorrect total (4 instead of 5) and an incorrect current coverage figure (3/4 instead of the correct 4/5).
option_notes.D: Wrong. Because the values 0 and negative numbers both fall in the SAME invalid partition (bandwidth <= 0), a single test case using either value is sufficient to exercise that one partition - there is no need for two separate test cases. This treats one partition as if it were two.

questions.distractor_note: Option D is a realistic trap: test-takers sometimes assume every distinct 'kind' of invalid input (zero vs. negative) needs its own test, but equivalence partitioning theory says any single value from a partition is representative of the whole partition - one test per partition is sufficient by definition.
questions.alt_wording: Given the same four quality tiers and reject-reading rule, if a tester wants to reach 100% equivalence partition coverage with the fewest possible test cases, how many test cases are needed in total, and what must the extra one(s) target?

questions.topic: Boundary Value Analysis - 2-Value vs 3-Value Detection Power
questions.question: An auto-insurance system should apply a low-mileage discount when a driver's annual mileage is at most 8,000 miles (mileage <= 8000). A developer mistakenly implements this rule as 'if (mileage == 8000) applyDiscount();' - meaning the discount is granted ONLY when mileage is exactly 8,000, and denied for every other value, including mileage well below 8,000. Using 3-value BVA at the 8,000-mile boundary, which test value exposes this defect, and why do the standard 2-value BVA test values fail to catch it?

options.A: mileage = 7,999 exposes the defect: the correct rule says a discount should be granted (7,999 <= 8,000), but the buggy code denies it (7,999 != 8,000). The 2-value tests, mileage = 8,000 and mileage = 8,001, both happen to match the correct behavior by coincidence, so they do not reveal the defect.
options.B: mileage = 8,001 exposes the defect, because it is above the boundary and should never receive a discount.
options.C: mileage = 8,000 exposes the defect, because it is the exact boundary value where the rule changes.
options.D: mileage = 16,000 exposes the defect, because it is far from the boundary and represents an extreme, out-of-range test value.

questions.why_correct: 3-value BVA at the 8,000-mile boundary tests three values: 7,999 (neighbor below), 8,000 (the boundary itself), and 8,001 (neighbor above). Checking each against both the correct rule (mileage <= 8000) and the buggy code (mileage == 8000): at 8,000, correct says 'discount' (true) and buggy also says 'discount' (8000==8000 is true) - they agree, no defect shown. At 8,001, correct says 'no discount' (false) and buggy also says 'no discount' (8001==8000 is false) - they agree again, no defect shown. Only at 7,999 do they disagree: correct says 'discount' (7999<=8000 is true) but buggy says 'no discount' (7999==8000 is false). This mismatch is what exposes the defect. Since the standard 2-value BVA set for this boundary is exactly {8,000, 8,001} - both of which coincidentally agree with the buggy code - 2-value BVA misses this defect entirely, while 3-value BVA's extra neighbor (7,999) catches it. This mirrors the syllabus's own example of why 3-value BVA is more rigorous than 2-value BVA: a boundary condition mistakenly coded as an equality check can pass every 2-value BVA test while still being wrong for the entire rest of the valid range.

option_notes.A: Correct, as shown in the worked comparison above: 7,999 is the one BVA-derived value where correct and buggy behavior diverge.
option_notes.B: Wrong. At mileage = 8,001, both the correct rule (8001 <= 8000 is false, so no discount) and the buggy code (8001 == 8000 is false, so no discount) agree - no defect is revealed here, even though 8,001 is a legitimate 2-value and 3-value BVA test point.
option_notes.C: Wrong, and this is the most tempting-looking answer since 8,000 IS the named boundary. But at exactly mileage = 8,000, both the correct rule (8000 <= 8000 is true) and the buggy code (8000 == 8000 is true) agree that a discount should be granted - so testing the boundary value itself does not reveal this particular defect.
option_notes.D: Wrong. While mileage = 16,000 does correctly receive 'no discount' from both the correct rule and the buggy code (both agree, so no defect shown), it is not a value derived from boundary value analysis at all - BVA test values come from the boundaries of partitions, not arbitrary values far from any boundary.

questions.distractor_note: Option C exploits the natural assumption that 'the boundary value' is always the one that best exposes a boundary-related defect. Here, the specific coding error (using == instead of <=) happens to still work correctly at the exact boundary value, so it takes the neighbor just below the boundary - a genuine 3-value BVA coverage item - to catch it. This directly illustrates the syllabus's point that 3-value BVA can detect defects that 2-value BVA overlooks.
questions.alt_wording: For the same mis-coded 'mileage == 8000' rule, list the three coverage items required for 3-value BVA at this boundary, and identify which one is the ONLY value (among all values tested by 2-value or 3-value BVA) that produces a different result between the correct and the buggy implementation.

questions.topic: Decision Table Testing - Feasible Rules and Coverage
questions.question: An online restaurant ordering system applies discounts based on three Boolean conditions: 'Customer is a loyalty member' (T/F), 'Order placed during happy hour' (T/F), and 'Valid promo code entered' (T/F). The system's checkout page automatically disables promo code entry whenever an order is placed during happy hour, so it is infeasible for both 'happy hour = True' and 'valid promo code entered = True' to occur together in the same rule, regardless of loyalty status. The team has already run test cases exercising 4 distinct feasible rules. What is the current decision table coverage, and how many more test cases are needed to reach 100%?

options.A: 66.7% coverage (4 of 6 feasible rules); 2 more test cases are needed
options.B: 50% coverage (4 of 8 total rules); 4 more test cases are needed
options.C: 66.7% coverage; no more test cases are needed, because infeasible combinations already reduce the required testing effort enough
options.D: 80% coverage (4 of 5 feasible rules); 1 more test case is needed

questions.why_correct: With 3 Boolean conditions, a full limited-entry decision table has 2^3 = 8 columns (rules). The infeasible combination is 'happy hour = True AND promo code = True,' which occurs regardless of loyalty status, i.e., for 2 of the 8 columns (loyalty = True with that combination, and loyalty = False with that combination). Removing those 2 infeasible columns leaves 8 - 2 = 6 feasible columns. Per the syllabus, decision table coverage items are the columns containing feasible combinations of conditions, and coverage is measured as exercised feasible columns divided by total feasible columns. With 4 of the 6 feasible rules already exercised, coverage = 4/6 = 66.7%, and 2 more feasible rules still need a test case each to reach 100%.

option_notes.A: Correct. 8 total combinations minus 2 infeasible ones (happy-hour-and-promo-code-together, for each loyalty value) leaves 6 feasible rules; 4/6 exercised = 66.7%, with 2 rules remaining.
option_notes.B: Wrong. This uses the full 8 rules as the denominator instead of the 6 feasible rules, ignoring that decision table coverage is explicitly measured against feasible columns only, not the full un-simplified table. It also overstates the number of tests still needed as a result.
option_notes.C: Wrong. Removing infeasible columns reduces the table size, but it does not exempt the remaining feasible columns from needing coverage - all 6 feasible rules must still be exercised by at least one test case each to reach 100% coverage; only 4 have been so far.
option_notes.D: Wrong. This undercounts the infeasible combinations, effectively removing only 1 rule instead of correctly identifying that BOTH loyalty-member values (True and False) make the happy-hour-and-promo-code combination infeasible, which removes 2 columns, not 1.

questions.distractor_note: Option B represents the single most common decision-table mistake: forgetting to exclude infeasible combinations before calculating coverage percentage. Always identify and remove infeasible columns first, then compute coverage against that reduced, feasible total.
questions.alt_wording: If this same restaurant discount decision table needed 100% coverage using the minimum number of test cases, how many total test cases would that require, and why is that number less than 2^3 = 8?

questions.topic: State Transition Testing - Valid Transitions vs All Transitions Coverage
questions.question: A smart door lock cycles through 4 states (Locked, Unlocking, Unlocked, Locking) via exactly 4 valid transitions, forming a single cycle. Its state table also explicitly identifies 3 additional invalid transition attempts (e.g., pressing the lock button while already Locked), giving 7 transitions in total. A test suite exercises all 4 valid transitions and attempts 1 of the 3 invalid transitions. What valid transitions coverage and all transitions coverage does this test suite achieve?

options.A: Valid transitions coverage = 100% (4 of 4 valid transitions); all transitions coverage = approximately 71.4% (5 of 7 total transitions)
options.B: Valid transitions coverage = 100%; all transitions coverage = 100%, because achieving full valid transitions coverage automatically guarantees full all transitions coverage
options.C: Valid transitions coverage = approximately 57.1% (4 of 7); all transitions coverage = approximately 71.4% (5 of 7)
options.D: Valid transitions coverage = 100%; all transitions coverage = 80% (4 of 5 total transitions)

questions.why_correct: Per the syllabus, valid transitions coverage (0-switch coverage) is measured as exercised valid transitions divided by the TOTAL NUMBER OF VALID transitions only: 4/4 = 100%. All transitions coverage is measured as exercised valid-and-invalid transitions divided by the total number of valid AND invalid transitions shown in the state table: (4 valid + 1 invalid exercised) / (4 valid + 3 invalid total) = 5/7 = approximately 71.4%. The syllabus also states the relationship runs one way only: achieving full ALL transitions coverage guarantees full valid transitions coverage (and full all states coverage), but the reverse is not true - full valid transitions coverage does NOT guarantee full all transitions coverage, since invalid transitions can remain completely unexercised, as they do here (only 1 of 3 invalid transitions was attempted).

option_notes.A: Correct: valid transitions coverage divides by the valid-transition total (4/4=100%); all transitions coverage divides by the combined total (5/7 is approximately 71.4%).
option_notes.B: Wrong. This states the implication backwards. The syllabus says full ALL transitions coverage guarantees full valid transitions coverage - not the other way around. Here, 100% valid transitions coverage is achieved while 2 of the 3 invalid transitions remain completely untested, so all transitions coverage is well below 100%.
option_notes.C: Wrong. This divides the 4 exercised valid transitions by the combined total of 7 transitions (valid + invalid), rather than dividing by the total number of valid transitions alone (4). Valid transitions coverage is defined against valid transitions only, not the full transition count.
option_notes.D: Wrong. This assumes only 1 invalid transition exists in total (giving a total of 4 valid + 1 invalid = 5), when the state table actually identifies 3 invalid transitions, only 1 of which was exercised.

questions.distractor_note: Option B tests a specific, easily-reversed syllabus relationship: full all-transitions coverage implies full valid-transitions coverage, but achieving 100% valid transitions coverage says nothing about how many invalid transitions were covered, since invalid transitions aren't counted in that metric at all.
questions.alt_wording: For the same door-lock state model, if the team wants to reach a minimum requirement suitable for mission- or safety-critical software (per the syllabus), which coverage criterion must they target, and how many more invalid transitions must be exercised from the current test suite to achieve it?

questions.question: Which of the following statements about equivalence partitioning, according to the syllabus, is FALSE?

options.A: Equivalence partitions must not overlap and must be non-empty sets.
options.B: To achieve 100% equivalence partitioning coverage, only the valid partitions need to be exercised; exercising invalid partitions is optional.
options.C: Equivalence partitions may be continuous or discrete, ordered or unordered, and finite or infinite.
options.D: Each Choice coverage requires exercising each partition from each set of partitions at least once, but does not take combinations of partitions into account.

questions.why_correct: The syllabus is explicit that 'to achieve 100% coverage with this test technique, test cases must exercise all identified partitions (including invalid partitions) by covering each partition at least once.' Invalid partitions are not optional for 100% coverage - they are coverage items just like valid partitions. Statement B contradicts this directly, making it the FALSE statement and therefore the correct answer to this question.

option_notes.A: True statement (not the answer). The syllabus states partitions 'must not overlap and must be non-empty sets.'
option_notes.B: False statement (this is the answer). Invalid partitions ARE required for 100% equivalence partitioning coverage, not optional - the syllabus explicitly includes them in the coverage formula.
option_notes.C: True statement (not the answer). The syllabus states partitions 'may be continuous or discrete, ordered or unordered, finite or infinite.'
option_notes.D: True statement (not the answer). The syllabus defines Each Choice coverage exactly this way: it requires exercising each partition from each set at least once, without accounting for combinations of partitions.

questions.alt_wording: All of the following are true about equivalence partitioning EXCEPT: (same four options, reworded stem)

questions.question: A traffic-light controller function contains 25 executable statements. A test suite exercises 19 of them. What statement coverage does this test suite achieve?

options.A: 76% (19 divided by 25)
options.B: 95% (mistakenly treating 20, not 25, as the total number of executable statements)
options.C: 24% (the percentage of statements NOT exercised, mistaken for the coverage figure itself)
options.D: 19% (misreading the raw count of exercised statements as if it were already a percentage)

questions.why_correct: Per the syllabus, statement coverage is measured as the number of statements exercised by the test cases divided by the total number of executable statements in the code, expressed as a percentage. Here that is 19 / 25 = 0.76 = 76%.

option_notes.B: Wrong. This results from using an incorrect total (20 instead of the stated 25 executable statements), which is a data-entry/miscounting error rather than a valid alternative calculation.
option_notes.C: Wrong. 24% is the percentage of statements that were NOT exercised (6 of 25 = 24%), which is the complement of the coverage figure, not the coverage figure itself. A common mistake is calculating the 'gap' and reporting it as if it were the coverage achieved.
option_notes.D: Wrong. This simply restates the raw exercised-statement count (19) as a percentage without dividing by the total number of executable statements at all.

questions.alt_wording: If this same 25-statement function needs to reach at least 90% statement coverage, what is the minimum number of statements that must be exercised, and how many additional statements beyond the 19 already covered does that require?

questions.topic: Statement Coverage vs Branch Coverage - Practical Divergence

options.A: 100% statement coverage; 50% branch coverage
options.B: 100% statement coverage; 100% branch coverage, because every executable statement in the function was reached
options.C: 50% statement coverage; 50% branch coverage
options.D: 100% statement coverage; 0% branch coverage, because a single test case can never exercise a branch outcome

questions.why_correct: With isPremiumMember = true, execution runs statement 1 (fee = 10), enters the if block and runs statement 2 (fee = 0), then runs statement 3 (processPayment). All 3 executable statements run at least once, giving 100% statement coverage. However, the 'if' decision has two possible outcomes - true and false - and only the true outcome was exercised; the false outcome (a non-premium member, where statement 2 is skipped) was never tested. Branch coverage = branches exercised / total branches = 1/2 = 50%. This demonstrates the syllabus's point that '100% statement coverage does not ensure that all the decision logic has been tested... it may not exercise all the branches.'

option_notes.A: Correct, as derived above: all statements execute (100%), but only one of the two branch outcomes of the if-decision is exercised (50%).
option_notes.B: Wrong. This is the classic misconception that statement coverage and branch coverage always move together. Reaching every statement is not the same as exercising every decision outcome - the false path of the 'if' was never taken by this single test case, so branch coverage is only 50%, not 100%.
option_notes.C: Wrong. Statement 2 (fee = 0) DOES execute, because isPremiumMember is true, so the if block runs. All 3 statements execute, giving 100% statement coverage, not 50%. This option incorrectly assumes the if body was skipped.
option_notes.D: Wrong. A single test case with isPremiumMember = true DOES exercise the true outcome of the branch (1 of 2 branches, or 50%) - it just fails to exercise the false outcome. Branch coverage is not automatically 0% just because only one test case was run; it depends on which specific outcomes that test case happens to trigger.

questions.distractor_note: Option B is the most tempting wrong answer because in simple, branch-free code, statement coverage and branch coverage genuinely do coincide. This example is deliberately chosen with a single conditional to show a case where they diverge: statement coverage reaches 100% while branch coverage is still only 50%, since branch coverage subsumes statement coverage but not vice versa (per the syllabus: 'branch coverage subsumes statement coverage... but not vice versa').
questions.alt_wording: What is the minimum number of additional test cases needed to raise this test suite to 100% branch coverage, and what input value would that test case need?

questions.topic: Value and Limits of White-Box Testing - Defects of Omission
questions.question: A tax-calculation module's requirements specify that a luxury-tax surcharge must be applied to purchases over $10,000. However, the developer never implemented this rule at all - no code path for it exists anywhere in the module. A team then achieves 100% statement coverage and 100% branch coverage on the module through white-box testing, yet the missing surcharge rule is never detected. What does the syllabus identify as the BEST explanation for this?

options.A: White-box testing is based on the code that exists, so it cannot detect defects caused by requirements that were never implemented at all - a limitation the syllabus calls defects of omission
options.B: White-box testing always achieves lower coverage than black-box testing for financial calculations, which is why the missing rule went undetected
options.C: 100% branch coverage is not actually achievable for modules involving monetary thresholds, so the reported coverage figures must be inaccurate
options.D: The team should have used decision table testing instead of white-box testing, since decision tables always catch every missing business rule

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states a specific weakness of white-box test techniques: 'if the software does not implement one or more requirements, white-box testing may not detect the resulting defects of omission.' Because white-box techniques derive test cases from the code's actual structure, a requirement with no corresponding code simply has nothing for the coverage-based tests to exercise - 100% statement and branch coverage only describes how thoroughly the EXISTING code was tested, not whether all required behavior exists.

option_notes.A: Correct - directly matches the syllabus's stated weakness of white-box testing: defects of omission (missing requirements) are invisible to a technique that only analyzes existing code structure.
option_notes.B: Wrong. Coverage levels achieved by white-box vs. black-box testing are not compared or ranked this way anywhere in the syllabus, and this claim doesn't explain why a completely missing code path was never flagged - the real issue is that there was no code to cover, not a coverage-level shortfall.
option_notes.C: Wrong. Nothing in the syllabus suggests 100% branch coverage is unachievable for financial modules; this is an unsupported, fabricated claim that doesn't address the actual cause (a missing requirement).
option_notes.D: Wrong. While black-box techniques like decision table testing are indeed well suited to checking business rules against a specification (and could plausibly have caught this specific gap), the syllabus does not claim decision tables 'always' catch every missing rule, and the question is asking specifically about a documented LIMITATION of white-box testing, not a technique-substitution recommendation.

questions.alt_wording: Why can a module pass 100% statement coverage AND 100% branch coverage through white-box testing while still failing to implement one of its documented requirements?

questions.topic: Error Guessing (Fault Attacks) vs Checklist-Based vs Exploratory Testing
questions.question: Before testing a new document-upload feature, a tester recalls that on three previous projects, upload features consistently failed whenever users selected filenames containing special characters (e.g., '#', '&', emoji) or filenames longer than 255 characters. Based on this recollection, the tester writes a short list of these specific known problem patterns and deliberately designs test cases targeting them before testing begins. Which test technique is the tester applying, and what is this specific way of applying it called?

options.A: Error guessing, specifically a fault attack - a list of possible errors, defects, and failures is created in advance from experience, then used to design targeted tests
options.B: Exploratory testing, specifically session-based testing, where tests are designed, executed, and evaluated simultaneously while learning about the test object
options.C: Checklist-based testing, since the tester is working from a predefined list of items
options.D: Decision table testing, since multiple filename conditions are being combined to determine expected behavior

questions.why_correct: The syllabus describes error guessing as anticipating errors, defects, and failures based on the tester's knowledge, including 'how the application has worked in the past' and 'the types of failures that have occurred in other, similar applications.' It specifically names fault attacks as a way to implement error guessing: 'this test technique requires the tester to create or acquire a list of possible errors, defects and failures, and to design tests that will identify defects associated with the errors.' The tester's list of specific past-failure patterns (special characters, overlong filenames), built from direct experience on prior projects, matches this definition precisely.

option_notes.A: Correct - the tester is drawing on direct past-project experience to build a targeted list of anticipated failure patterns, which is the textbook definition of a fault attack within error guessing.
option_notes.B: Wrong. Exploratory testing designs, executes, and evaluates tests SIMULTANEOUSLY while learning about the test object in real time. Here, the tester's list was compiled BEFORE testing began, based on prior knowledge - the defining trait of error guessing, not the concurrent discover-as-you-go nature of exploratory testing.
option_notes.C: Wrong, though tempting since both techniques involve a 'list.' The syllabus describes checklist-based testing as using broad, often question-phrased, repeatable test conditions (e.g., about requirements, interface properties, or quality characteristics) intended for consistent reuse across testing efforts. The tester's list here is instead a targeted set of specific known defect patterns drawn from past failure experience - the defining trait of error guessing/fault attacks, not a general-purpose checklist.
option_notes.D: Wrong. Decision table testing derives test cases from combinations of Boolean or multi-valued conditions producing defined outcomes (e.g., business rules). There is no combination-of-conditions logic being modeled here - just a list of specific input patterns known to have caused failures before.

questions.distractor_note: Option C is the trickiest distractor because checklist-based testing and error guessing/fault attacks both involve working from a pre-built list, and the syllabus discusses them in adjacent sections. The distinguishing factor is the SOURCE and PURPOSE of the list: checklists tend to be broad, reusable, question-style conditions for consistency across many test efforts, while a fault attack's list is a targeted set of specific anticipated defects drawn from the tester's own experience of what actually failed before.
questions.alt_wording: A tester who has worked on several previous e-commerce sites recalls that discount codes have often failed to combine correctly with free-shipping promotions, and specifically designs a test case to try that exact combination. What is this approach called, and how would it differ from checklist-based testing applied to the same feature?

questions.question: A test team structures its investigative testing of a new voice-assistant app into fixed one-hour time-boxed sessions. Before each session, the tester receives a short written mission statement describing what to investigate (e.g., 'investigate how the assistant behaves with overlapping voice commands'). During the session, the tester simultaneously decides what to try, executes it, and evaluates the result, without following any pre-scripted steps. Afterward, the tester and a product stakeholder meet to discuss what was found. In official ISTQB terminology, what are the 'mission statement' and the after-session discussion respectively called?

options.A: Test charter, and debriefing
options.B: Test condition, and test completion report
options.C: Checklist, and retrospective
options.D: Test procedure, and exit criteria review

questions.why_correct: The syllabus describes session-based exploratory testing exactly this way: 'The tester uses a test charter containing test objectives to guide the testing... The test session is usually followed by a debriefing that involves a discussion between the tester and stakeholders interested in the test results of the test session.'

option_notes.A: Correct - matches the syllabus's own terminology for session-based exploratory testing precisely.
option_notes.B: Wrong. A test condition is a general term for any testable aspect of a component or system (identified using any test technique, not specific to exploratory testing), and a test completion report is a formal end-of-testing summary document, not an informal post-session discussion.
option_notes.C: Wrong. A checklist is the artifact used specifically in checklist-based testing, a different experience-based technique from exploratory testing. A retrospective is a broader, separate practice (discussed under Chapter 2's SDLC content) held to improve the team's overall process at the end of an iteration or project, not a single exploratory session's debriefing.
option_notes.D: Wrong. A test procedure specifies the sequence in which test cases should be executed, typically for scripted testing - essentially the opposite of exploratory testing's unscripted, discovery-driven nature. An exit criteria review is unrelated to a session debriefing.

questions.alt_wording: What term does the syllabus use for the guiding document that lists test objectives at the start of an exploratory testing session, and what happens right after the session ends?

questions.topic: Checklist-Based Testing - Maintenance and Length Pitfalls
questions.question: A QA lead has used the same 15-item usability checklist, unchanged, to test every release of a banking app for three years. Recently, several high-severity usability defects have slipped through even though every checklist item still passes on every release. According to the syllabus, what is the MOST likely explanation, and what should the QA lead do about it?

options.A: Checklist entries can gradually become less effective over time as developers learn to avoid the errors the checklist was built to catch; the checklist should be regularly updated based on defect analysis, including new entries for newly found high-severity defects
options.B: The checklist approach is fundamentally unsuitable for usability testing and should be replaced entirely with exploratory testing
options.C: The checklist has too few items; the QA lead should expand it to at least 50 items to increase its defect-detection power
options.D: Checklist-based testing always loses effectiveness after its first year of use and should be discarded and rewritten after every major release, regardless of what defects have occurred

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states: 'Some checklist entries may gradually become less effective over time because the developers will learn to avoid making the same errors. New entries may also need to be added to reflect newly found high severity defects. Therefore, checklists should be regularly updated based on defect analysis.' This exactly matches the scenario: a static, unchanged checklist stops catching new categories of defects as developers adapt, and the fix is regular defect-analysis-driven updates, not abandonment or indiscriminate expansion.

option_notes.A: Correct - matches the syllabus's specific guidance on why checklists lose effectiveness over time and how to address it (regular, defect-analysis-driven updates).
option_notes.B: Wrong. The syllabus explicitly notes checklists can support non-functional testing including usability testing (citing Nielsen's usability heuristics as an example), so checklist-based testing is not described as unsuitable for this purpose - it simply needs maintenance.
option_notes.C: Wrong. The syllabus warns the opposite: 'care should be taken to avoid letting the checklist become too long.' Arbitrarily expanding to 50 items contradicts this explicit guidance and is not the recommended fix for a stale checklist.
option_notes.D: Wrong. The syllabus describes checklist staleness as a gradual, defect-analysis-driven maintenance issue, not a rule that checklists automatically expire after a fixed time period or must be discarded on every release regardless of actual findings. This option fabricates a rigid schedule the syllabus does not state.

questions.distractor_note: Options C and D both overcorrect in opposite directions - C says 'add much more,' D says 'throw it away and start over on a schedule' - while the syllabus's actual guidance is a moderate, evidence-based one: keep the checklist reasonably sized but periodically refresh its content based on which defects are actually being found (and missed).
questions.alt_wording: Why might a checklist that catches every defect it lists nonetheless become an unreliable indicator of software quality over time, and what does the syllabus recommend as the remedy?

questions.question: A team practices ATDD for a user story: 'As a customer, I want to apply a discount code at checkout so that I pay a reduced price.' Its acceptance criteria cover a valid code being applied correctly, an expired code being rejected, promo codes not stacking with other active promotions, and checkout completing within 2 seconds even when a code is applied. According to the syllabus's description of ATDD, in what order should the team typically create its test cases during test design?

options.A: First, positive test cases confirming correct behavior with no errors (e.g., a valid code is applied correctly); then negative test cases (e.g., an expired code is rejected, stacking is blocked); finally, test cases covering non-functional quality characteristics (e.g., the 2-second checkout performance criterion)
options.B: First negative test cases, to surface defects as early as possible; then positive test cases; then non-functional test cases
options.C: Non-functional test cases first, since performance is treated as the team's highest business risk; then positive test cases; then negative test cases
options.D: Positive and negative test cases should be created together, interleaved rule by rule; non-functional criteria are covered incidentally within those same test cases rather than as separate ones

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states the typical ATDD ordering explicitly: 'Typically, the first test cases are positive, confirming the correct behavior without exceptions or error conditions... After the positive test cases are done, the team should perform negative testing. Finally, the team should cover non-functional quality characteristics.' Applied to this story, that means: valid-code application first, then expired-code/stacking-rejection cases, then the 2-second performance criterion last.

option_notes.A: Correct - matches the syllabus's stated order: positive, then negative, then non-functional.
option_notes.B: Wrong. This reverses the syllabus's stated order. Positive test cases (confirming the sequence of activities executed when everything goes as expected) are created first, not negative ones.
option_notes.C: Wrong. Nothing in the syllabus's description of ATDD prioritizes non-functional test cases first based on perceived business risk; the stated order is positive, then negative, then non-functional, regardless of risk framing (risk-based prioritization is a separate topic covered in Chapter 5, not part of the ATDD ordering guidance).
option_notes.D: Wrong. The syllabus treats non-functional quality characteristics as their own distinct, later step in ATDD test design, not something folded incidentally into positive/negative functional test cases.

questions.alt_wording: In ATDD, why does the syllabus recommend writing the 'happy path' test cases before the error-condition and non-functional ones, rather than mixing them in whatever order the team encounters them during the specification workshop?

questions.topic: Collaborative User Story Writing - Stakeholder Testability Signal
questions.question: During collaborative story writing for a hospital's medication-management system, the team drafts a user story: 'As a clinician, I want to view a patient's medication history so that I can avoid prescribing conflicting drugs.' When asked how they would test this story, a clinician stakeholder is unable to describe any concrete way to verify it. According to the syllabus, what does this MOST likely indicate?

options.A: The user story may not be clear enough, or it may not reflect something the stakeholder actually finds valuable, or the stakeholder may simply need help understanding how to test it
options.B: The user story violates the 'Independent' criterion of INVEST and must be split into smaller, unrelated stories immediately
options.C: The story provides no genuine business value and should be removed from the backlog immediately
options.D: The team should proceed directly to writing acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format, since that format always resolves testability confusion

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states directly: 'If a stakeholder does not know how to test a user story, this may indicate that the user story is not clear enough, or that it does not reflect something valuable to them, or that the stakeholder just needs help in testing (Wake 2003).' All three possibilities are given together as the likely explanations - the team's next step should be to investigate which of these applies, through further collaborative conversation, not to jump to a single conclusion.

option_notes.A: Correct - reproduces all three syllabus-stated possible explanations for a stakeholder's inability to describe how to test their own story.
option_notes.B: Wrong. 'Independent' in INVEST concerns whether a story can be developed and delivered without being tightly coupled to other stories - it is unrelated to whether a stakeholder personally understands how to test the story's behavior.
option_notes.C: Wrong - an overreaction not supported by the syllabus. One of the three stated possibilities is that the story simply isn't clear enough or the stakeholder needs help testing it; the syllabus does not conclude that testability confusion alone proves an absence of business value, and it does not recommend immediate removal.
option_notes.D: Wrong. Switching to a specific acceptance-criteria format (Given/When/Then, i.e., BDD-style scenario-oriented format) is not stated anywhere in the syllabus as a guaranteed fix for this kind of testability confusion; the actual underlying issue (unclear story, low perceived value, or a skills gap) needs to be identified and addressed directly.

questions.alt_wording: A product owner cannot explain how they would verify that a new user story has been correctly implemented. What three possible root causes does the syllabus suggest the team should consider?

questions.question: Two expert-based estimation techniques described in the syllabus both rely on the judgment of multiple experts, but they differ in method. A test manager for a logistics company's route-optimization module wants an estimate produced in ONE round, where three specific figures - the most optimistic, most likely, and most pessimistic effort - are combined using a weighted formula that also yields a measure of estimation error. Which estimation technique does this describe, and how does it differ from Wideband Delphi?

options.A: Wideband Delphi; both techniques use the same single-round weighted formula E = (a + 4m + b) / 6
options.B: Three-point estimation; unlike Wideband Delphi, it uses one round of three weighted figures combined by a formula, rather than repeated rounds of anonymous re-estimation and discussion until the experts converge
options.C: Estimation based on ratios; unlike Wideband Delphi, it derives the estimate from a fixed historical development-to-test ratio rather than expert judgment
options.D: Extrapolation; unlike Wideband Delphi, it uses early project measurements rather than expert opinions

questions.why_correct: The described technique - three specific figures (optimistic a, most likely m, pessimistic b) combined via a weighted formula E = (a + 4m + b) / 6 in a single round, with SD = (b - a) / 6 as the error measure - is exactly three-point estimation as defined in the syllabus. Wideband Delphi differs because it is an iterative, expert-based technique: each expert estimates in isolation, results are compared, and if estimates deviate beyond agreed boundaries, the experts discuss and re-estimate (again in isolation) until consensus is reached. It has no single weighted formula for combining figures.

option_notes.A: Incorrect. Wideband Delphi does not use a fixed weighted formula at all - it reaches an estimate through repeated rounds of isolated estimation and group discussion until consensus, not through a mathematical combination of three figures.
option_notes.B: Correct. This is three-point estimation, and the explanation correctly contrasts its single-round formula-based approach with Wideband Delphi's iterative consensus process.
option_notes.C: Incorrect. Estimation based on ratios is a metrics-based technique using historical data (e.g., a 3:2 development-to-test ratio from past projects), not an expert-judgment technique involving optimistic/likely/pessimistic figures.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. Extrapolation is also metrics-based, using measurements gathered early in the current project (e.g., averaging the last few iterations' effort), not expert opinions about a, m, and b.

questions.distractor_note: Option A is the most tempting distractor because both three-point estimation and Wideband Delphi are expert-based techniques, which can make a test-taker assume they share the same mechanics. The real differentiator the syllabus draws is process shape: three-point estimation is a single-round calculation, while Wideband Delphi is a multi-round consensus-building process (of which Planning Poker is a common Agile variant) with no fixed formula.
questions.alt_wording: A team wants a consensus estimate reached through several rounds, where each expert first estimates in isolation and any outlying estimates are discussed before a new round of isolated re-estimation - is this Wideband Delphi or three-point estimation, and why?

questions.question: A test team for POS terminal firmware orders its regression suite like this: the first test case chosen is the one that, by itself, achieves the most statement coverage. Every test case chosen after that is the one that adds the largest amount of NEW statement coverage not already achieved by any previously selected test case. The syllabus has a specific name for this ordering approach - what is it?

options.A: Risk-based prioritization
options.B: Requirements-based prioritization
options.C: Coverage-based prioritization (the basic form, where each test case is ranked independently by its own coverage figure)
options.D: Additional coverage prioritization, a variant of coverage-based prioritization in which each subsequent test case is the one achieving the highest ADDITIONAL coverage

questions.why_correct: The syllabus explicitly names this exact approach 'additional coverage prioritization': after the first test case (chosen for the highest coverage on its own), each subsequent test case is selected because it achieves the highest additional coverage relative to what has already been covered. This is presented as a specific variant of coverage-based prioritization, distinct from the basic form.

option_notes.A: Incorrect. Risk-based prioritization orders test execution by the results of risk analysis, executing test cases covering the most important risks first - coverage figures are not the basis here.
option_notes.B: Incorrect. Requirements-based prioritization orders test execution by stakeholder-defined requirement priorities, not by statement coverage.
option_notes.C: Incorrect but tempting. Plain coverage-based prioritization ranks test cases independently by their own coverage (e.g., always run the highest-coverage test cases first), which could pick two heavily overlapping tests back to back. The scenario specifically re-evaluates 'not yet covered' after each selection, which is the additional coverage variant, not the basic form.
option_notes.D: Correct - matches the syllabus's description and name for this exact selection process.

questions.distractor_note: Option C is the key trap: it is the correct parent category (coverage-based) but the wrong specific variant. The scenario's re-evaluation of remaining uncovered code after each pick is precisely what distinguishes 'additional coverage prioritization' from the basic coverage-based approach, which does not account for overlap between already-selected tests.
questions.alt_wording: Which prioritization strategy avoids selecting two test cases that mostly re-cover the same code, by always choosing next the test case that adds the most NEW coverage compared to what has already been selected?

questions.topic: Primary Purpose of a Test Plan
questions.question: A test manager preparing a new test plan for a government benefits portal is asked by a stakeholder: 'What is this document actually for?' According to the syllabus, which of the following BEST describes the primary purpose of a test plan?

options.A: To guarantee that the released software will contain zero defects
options.B: To document the means and schedule for achieving the test objectives, and to serve as a means of communication with team members and other stakeholders
options.C: To replace the organization's test policy and test strategy with project-specific rules
options.D: To list every individual test case that will be executed during the project

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states that a test plan documents the means and schedule for achieving test objectives, helps ensure performed test activities meet established criteria, serves as a means of communication with stakeholders, and demonstrates adherence to (or deviation from) the test policy and test strategy. Option B captures this core purpose.

option_notes.A: Incorrect. No document can guarantee zero defects; this also contradicts the 'absence of defects is a fallacy' idea from the testing principles - defects can still slip through even with a thorough test plan.
option_notes.B: Correct - matches the syllabus's stated purpose of a test plan.
option_notes.C: Incorrect. A test plan demonstrates that testing will adhere to the existing test policy and test strategy, or explains why it will deviate from them - it does not replace those higher-level documents.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. Individual test cases are testware typically documented in separate test case specifications produced during test design/implementation, not listed line-by-line inside the test plan itself, which instead addresses scope, approach, risks, schedule, and similar higher-level content.

questions.alt_wording: Which of the following is NOT one of the syllabus-listed purposes of a test plan? (turns this into a negative-style question using the same four candidate purposes)

questions.topic: Project Risk vs Product Risk Classification
questions.question:
A supply-chain visibility platform project has raised four concerns:

I. The platform's geolocation module reports the wrong warehouse for roughly 1 in 200 shipments.
II. The only integration specialist familiar with the customs-clearance API has resigned mid-project.
III. The chosen test automation tool has poor support for the platform's newer UI framework, slowing down test script creation.
IV. Under peak load, the platform's dashboard takes over 30 seconds to refresh, well outside the non-functional requirement.

Which combination correctly classifies these as project risks vs product risks, according to the syllabus's examples?

options.A: I and IV are product risks; II and III are project risks
options.B: I and II are product risks; III and IV are project risks
options.C: I, III, and IV are product risks; II is a project risk
options.D: All four are product risks, since they all ultimately affect the delivered platform

questions.why_correct: Item I (wrong functionality/incorrect output) and item IV (inadequate response time) are both explicitly listed by the syllabus as examples of product risks - they relate to the product's own quality characteristics. Item II (staff shortage/people issue) and item III (poor tool support, listed under project risks' 'technical issues') are both explicitly listed as examples of project risks - they relate to the project's ability to meet its schedule, budget, or scope, not the product's quality.

option_notes.A: Correct. Matches the syllabus's categorization: I and IV are product quality issues (wrong output, inadequate response time); II and III are issues with running the project itself (staffing, tooling).
option_notes.B: Incorrect. It swaps II into product risks, but a resigned specialist is a people issue explicitly listed under project risks, not a product quality characteristic.
option_notes.C: Incorrect. It places III (poor tool support) among the product risks, but the syllabus explicitly lists 'poor tool support' as a project risk example under technical issues, alongside scope creep - it affects the project's execution, not the software's own quality.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. This collapses the entire project risk vs product risk distinction; staffing and tooling problems affect the project's schedule/budget/scope, which is precisely the definition of a project risk, not a product risk.

questions.distractor_note: Option C is the most common trap: 'poor tool support' sounds like it concerns testing quality, tempting a reader to file it under product risk. But the syllabus is explicit that poor tool support is a project risk (a technical issue affecting the project), while inadequate response time IS a product risk because it is a product quality characteristic (performance efficiency).
questions.alt_wording: For each of four listed concerns on an aviation maintenance-logging project, state whether it is a project risk or a product risk, then pick the option with the fully correct grouping.

questions.topic: Risk Transfer vs Risk Mitigation by Testing
questions.question: For a maritime shipping-tracking system, the team identifies a product risk: the vessel position feed could report stale GPS coordinates during network handoffs. In response, the team purchases additional insurance to cover potential losses from cargo misrouted because of this issue, without changing the test approach at all. Which category of response to product risk does this represent?

options.A: Risk mitigation by testing, since resources are being spent to address the risk
options.B: Risk transfer, since the financial consequence of the risk is being shifted to a third party (the insurer) instead of being reduced through testing
options.C: Risk acceptance, since the team has decided to do nothing about the risk
options.D: Risk monitoring, since the team is tracking the risk's potential financial impact

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists several general response options to an analyzed product risk: risk mitigation by testing, risk acceptance, risk transfer, or a contingency plan. Purchasing insurance shifts the financial consequence of the risk to a third party (the insurer) rather than reducing the likelihood or impact through testing - this is the definition of risk transfer.

option_notes.A: Incorrect. Mitigation BY TESTING refers specifically to testing-related actions (selecting testers with the right skills, applying appropriate independence, performing reviews/static analysis, applying suitable test techniques and coverage, appropriate test types, dynamic/regression testing). Buying insurance is not a testing action, even though money is being spent.
option_notes.B: Correct - buying insurance transfers the financial consequence elsewhere, which is exactly what risk transfer means.
option_notes.C: Incorrect. Acceptance means consciously deciding to take no action and simply live with the risk. Here the team took an active step (purchasing insurance), so this is not acceptance.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. Risk monitoring is about checking whether mitigation actions remain effective, gathering more information to refine risk assessment, and spotting emerging risks - not shifting a risk's financial consequence to an insurer.

questions.distractor_note: Option C is the main trap because 'not changing the test approach' can look like doing nothing. But the team did take an active response - buying insurance - so it isn't acceptance. The distinguishing feature of transfer is that the consequence (not the likelihood or the testing approach) is being shifted elsewhere.
questions.alt_wording: A retailer's product risk of a payment-gateway outage during a promotion is handled by writing a contract clause making a subcontractor liable for related losses, instead of testing more thoroughly - name this response option and explain why it isn't mitigation by testing.

questions.topic: Risk Level - Equal Levels from Different Factor Combinations
questions.question:
For a renewable-energy grid-monitoring dashboard, product risk analysis quantitatively assesses two risks:
- Risk A: 'Incorrect solar-output readings displayed to operators' - likelihood 0.6, impact rated 4.
- Risk B: 'Dashboard fails to alert on a grid-frequency deviation' - likelihood 0.3, impact rated 8.

Using the quantitative approach (risk level = risk likelihood x risk impact), what can be concluded?

options.A: Risk A has a higher risk level than Risk B, so it should be prioritized above Risk B
options.B: Risk B has a higher risk level than Risk A, so it should be prioritized above Risk A
options.C: Risk A and Risk B have the same risk level (2.4), so despite their very different likelihood/impact profiles, neither is automatically prioritized over the other on risk level alone
options.D: Risk level cannot be calculated here because likelihood and impact must be expressed on the same 0-to-1 scale

questions.why_correct: Risk A: 0.6 x 4 = 2.4. Risk B: 0.3 x 8 = 2.4. Both risks produce the identical risk level despite having very different individual likelihood and impact values. In the quantitative approach, risk level is the product of the two factors combined, not either factor considered alone - so a low-likelihood/high-impact risk can carry exactly the same risk level as a high-likelihood/low-impact risk.

option_notes.A: Incorrect. 0.6 x 4 = 2.4, which is not higher than Risk B's 2.4 - the two are equal.
option_notes.B: Incorrect. 0.3 x 8 = 2.4, which is not higher than Risk A's 2.4 - the two are equal.
option_notes.C: Correct - both calculations yield 2.4, illustrating that risk level combines likelihood and impact multiplicatively rather than being driven by one factor alone.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. The syllabus defines risk likelihood as a probability strictly between 0 and 1, but risk impact is a separate severity-style rating (here, a scale where 4 and 8 are used) - the quantitative approach simply multiplies the two values as given; they are not required to share the same numeric scale.

questions.distractor_note: This question is designed to catch a reader who assumes 'higher impact automatically means higher risk level' (tempting toward B) or 'higher likelihood automatically means higher risk level' (tempting toward A). The syllabus's actual point is that risk level is the combined product of both attributes, so very different-looking risks can end up equally important.
questions.alt_wording: Risk C has likelihood 0.8 and impact 3; Risk D has likelihood 0.4 and impact 6. Using the quantitative approach, compare their risk levels and explain what this means for prioritization.

questions.topic: Test Metrics Categories - Coverage vs Risk Metrics
questions.question: A 5G core-network test team's dashboard shows two figures at the end of a test cycle: '94% of the approved requirements now have at least one passing test case' and 'residual risk level for the billing-reconciliation feature has dropped from High to Low.' According to the syllabus's categories of test metrics, these two figures respectively belong to which categories?

options.A: Both are coverage metrics, since both figures measure how thoroughly the system has been tested
options.B: Requirements coverage is a coverage metric; residual risk level is a risk metric
options.C: Requirements coverage is a product quality metric; residual risk level is a defect metric
options.D: Both are project progress metrics, since both are reported at the end of a test cycle

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists coverage metrics (e.g., requirements coverage, code coverage) and risk metrics (e.g., residual risk level) as two distinct, explicitly named categories of test metrics. The '94% requirements covered' figure is a coverage metric; the 'residual risk level' figure is a risk metric.

option_notes.A: Incorrect. Lumping both under 'coverage metrics' ignores that residual risk level is the syllabus's own dedicated example of a risk metric, a separate category.
option_notes.B: Correct - matches the syllabus's example lists for coverage metrics and risk metrics exactly.
option_notes.C: Incorrect but plausible-sounding. Product quality metrics cover things like availability, response time, and mean time to failure, not requirements coverage. Defect metrics cover counts/priorities of defects found or fixed, defect density, and defect detection percentage, not residual risk level.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. Project progress metrics cover task completion, resource usage, and test effort - not coverage percentages or risk levels. When a metric is reported doesn't determine which category it belongs to.

questions.distractor_note: Option C is the trickiest distractor because it correctly recognizes the two figures belong to different categories, but assigns the wrong category names - a reminder to memorize the syllabus's actual category examples rather than just knowing that categories exist.
questions.alt_wording: A dashboard reports 'code coverage: 81%' and 'defect density: 2.3 per KLOC.' Name the two metric categories these figures respectively belong to.

questions.topic: Content Unique to a Test Completion Report
questions.question: A bank's core-system migration project has just finished its final system-test cycle before go-live, and the team prepares its closing report. Which of the following is a typical element the syllabus lists for a TEST COMPLETION REPORT that does NOT also appear among the typical elements it lists for a routine TEST PROGRESS REPORT?

options.A: Test metrics gathered during the reporting period
options.B: New and changed risks identified during the period
options.C: Lessons learned that are relevant to the testing
options.D: Impediments encountered during testing and their workarounds

questions.why_correct: The syllabus's list of typical test completion report content includes 'lessons learned that are relevant to the testing' - this item does not appear in the syllabus's list of typical test progress report content. The other three items (test metrics, risk-related information, and impediments/workarounds) appear, in some form, in both lists.

option_notes.A: Incorrect as the answer - test metrics appear in both: progress reports include test metrics for the period, and completion reports include test metrics based on the accumulated progress reports.
option_notes.B: Incorrect as the answer - 'new and changed risks within testing period' is actually listed as a test PROGRESS report element. The completion report instead lists a related but different item, 'unmitigated risks, defects not fixed,' so this specific wording belongs to progress reports, not uniquely to completion reports.
option_notes.C: Correct - 'lessons learned' is listed by the syllabus only under test completion report content, not under test progress report content.
option_notes.D: Incorrect as the answer - impediments and their workarounds appear in both lists (progress reports: 'impediments for testing, and their workarounds'; completion reports: 'testing impediments and workarounds').

questions.distractor_note: This question is tricky because three of the four elements (metrics, risk information, impediments) appear in some form in BOTH report types, just phrased slightly differently between the two syllabus lists. 'Lessons learned' is the one element the syllabus reserves specifically for the completion report.
questions.alt_wording: Which of the following appears in the syllabus's list of typical test progress report content but is absent from its list of typical test completion report content? (correct answer would be 'testing planned for the next period')

questions.topic: Formal Change Control After Baseline Approval
questions.question: A genomics lab's sequencing-analysis software has a test environment configuration that was approved for testing and is now treated as a baseline under configuration management. A developer wants to upgrade one of the underlying libraries in that environment. According to the syllabus, what BEST describes what configuration management requires before this change can be made?

options.A: The change should go through a formal change control process, since a baseline can only be changed that way
options.B: The change can be made freely, as long as the developer documents it afterward in an email to the team
options.C: The change is blocked entirely, since baselines can never be changed once approved
options.D: The change only needs sign-off from the test manager, since configuration management is solely a testing responsibility

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states: 'If the configuration item is approved for testing, it becomes a baseline and can only be changed through a formal change control process.' Configuration management also keeps a record of changed configuration items when a new baseline is created, which is how it remains possible to revert to a previous baseline to reproduce earlier test results.

option_notes.A: Correct - matches the syllabus's wording exactly.
option_notes.B: Incorrect. Informal, after-the-fact documentation (like an email) is not a formal change control process; configuration management requires tracked, controlled changes, not free-form self-reporting.
option_notes.C: Incorrect. Baselines CAN be changed - just only through a formal change control process. They are not permanently frozen, and configuration management specifically supports reverting to an earlier baseline when needed.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. Configuration management supports testing but is a broader project/organizational discipline covering all configuration items (documentation, software, environments), not something restricted to sign-off by a test manager alone.

questions.distractor_note: Option C is a common overcorrection: readers remember that a baseline is 'locked' and conclude it can never change again, but the syllabus's actual point is that changes remain possible - they just must go through formal change control, which is also why it's possible to revert to an earlier baseline to reproduce previous test results.
questions.alt_wording: After a test environment is approved and becomes a baseline, describe what configuration management still allows regarding future changes to it, and what it prevents.

questions.question: A smart-agriculture company's test object spans irrigation-controller firmware, a cloud API, and a companion mobile app, each with its own test cases, test scripts, and test results. According to the syllabus, what does configuration management ensure about these related work products so that traceability can be maintained throughout the test process?

options.A: That each item is merged into a single combined document to avoid tracking multiple versions
options.B: That each item is uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes, and related to the other configuration items
options.C: That each item is retested from scratch every time any one of the three components changes
options.D: That each item is reviewed by a certified test manager before it can be used

questions.why_correct: The syllabus states that, to properly support testing, configuration management ensures all configuration items - including test items - are uniquely identified, version controlled, tracked for changes, and related to other configuration items, so that traceability can be maintained throughout the test process.

option_notes.A: Incorrect. Configuration management does not require merging distinct items into one document; it manages multiple separate configuration items and the relationships between them.
option_notes.B: Correct - matches the syllabus's wording on what CM ensures for traceability.
option_notes.C: Incorrect. Configuration management is about identification, version control, and change tracking, not a retesting policy. Deciding what needs retesting after a change is a separate concern (e.g., regression testing scope), not something configuration management itself dictates.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. Configuration management does not mandate review by a certified test manager; that describes a review/approval activity, not the function of configuration management.

questions.alt_wording: Why does configuration management matter for a test project with multiple interrelated components (e.g., firmware, an API, and a mobile app)?

questions.question:
While testing fleet-management software for agricultural equipment, a tester logs two defects:
- Defect 1: The rarely-used 'export maintenance history to CSV' feature crashes the whole application, but only a handful of users use it, and it will not be shown during an upcoming board demo.
- Defect 2: A minor dashboard label reads 'Feul Level' instead of 'Fuel Level' - a typo with no functional impact, but the marketing lead insists it be fixed before tomorrow's investor demo.

Which pair of ratings correctly reflects the syllabus's distinction between severity and priority for these two defects?

options.A: Defect 1: high severity, high priority; Defect 2: low severity, low priority
options.B: Defect 1: high severity (a crash is a serious functional impact), with priority set separately by how urgently it needs fixing; Defect 2: low severity (a cosmetic typo), but potentially high priority for the demo - severity measures degree of impact, while priority measures urgency to fix
options.C: Defect 1 and Defect 2 have the same severity and priority, since both were found during the same test cycle
options.D: Defect 1: low severity, high priority; Defect 2: high severity, low priority

questions.why_correct: The syllabus lists severity ('degree of impact on the interests of stakeholders or requirements') and priority ('priority to fix') as two separate fields on a defect report. They do not have to move together: Defect 1's crash is high severity regardless of how few users are affected or how urgently it needs fixing before the demo, while Defect 2's typo is low severity but can still be assigned high priority purely because of business context (the investor demo).

option_notes.A: Incorrect. This assumes severity and priority always correlate. Defect 2 being low severity does not force it to also be low priority - the business context (an investor demo) can make even a cosmetic issue urgent to fix.
option_notes.B: Correct - separates the two attributes properly and shows how they can diverge.
option_notes.C: Incorrect. When a defect was discovered has no bearing on its severity or priority ratings; these are independent, deliberately assigned attributes.
option_notes.D: Incorrect. This reverses Defect 1's severity - a full application crash is high severity because of its serious functional impact, regardless of how few users are affected by that particular feature.

questions.distractor_note: Option A represents the most common misconception - assuming severity and priority always correlate. The syllabus deliberately separates them (severity = degree of impact/harm; priority = urgency to fix) precisely because business or scheduling context, like an upcoming demo, can make a low-severity issue urgent, or leave a high-severity issue at lower priority if, for example, the affected feature is rarely used.
questions.alt_wording: A defect causes a rarely-used report to fail silently (little functional impact), but the CEO wants it fixed before tomorrow's board meeting. What does this illustrate about the relationship between severity and priority?

questions.topic: Defect Report Objectives and Status (Multiple Statements)
questions.question:
A tester at a warehouse-robotics company is asked to explain the point of the defect management process to a new hire. Consider the following statements:

I. A defect report's objectives, per the syllabus, include providing enough information for those responsible to resolve the issue, and providing a means of tracking the quality of the work product.
II. Every anomaly reported during dynamic testing is, by definition, a confirmed defect in the code.
III. A defect report's 'status' field can include values such as open, deferred, awaiting confirmation testing, and rejected.
IV. Defect reports are only useful during dynamic testing; anomalies found during static testing should not be handled through a similar process.

Which of the statements are TRUE?

options.A: I and III only
options.B: I, II, and III
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I, II, III, and IV
